hits.name: GREG ISENBERG
hits.hook: running a company nowadays feels kinda dystopian
hits.original_en:
running a company nowadays feels kinda dystopian

my team is 50+ people in 12 countries, but i talk to my agents more than my human teammates

- voice note to grokbot
- mattpocock/skills /grill-me so the agent interrogates the idea before anything gets built
- spec drops into linear through the linear mcp
- exa + firecrawl agent reads every competitor site, pricing page and changelog
- https://t.co/a5ARFnvSnA to find ideas and trends
- apify pulls g2, reddit and app store reviews
- prompt: "find the 10 complaints that show up most and quote the users"
- context7 so the agent reads the latest docs before it touches any api

the design

- claude code + paper mcp
- 4 versions of every screen before a single line of code
- pick pieces from 2, it merges them. diverge then converge
- frontend-design skill from anthropic/skills + our own design system skill
- cleanshot screenshots of any ui i like go straight in with "make it feel like this"

the build

- pingdotgg/t3code as the control surface for every agent, from my phone too
- stablyai/orca runs a fleet of agents in parallel, each in its own git worktree
- graphify maps the whole codebase into a knowledge graph so agents navigate instead of guess
- headroom compresses tool outputs before they hit the model, so tokens go 20-95% further
- lsp plugins so the agent sees types and errors like an ide does
- security guidance hook flags risky edits before they land
- supabase mcp for the database, stripe for billing
- github mcp opens the pr, vercel spins up a preview
- loops run overnight, i check what shipped over coffee

the user testing

- lightpanda as the headless browser, way lighter than chromium so you can run hundreds at once
- agents click every flow on the preview like a first-time user
- one persona is impatient, one is confused, one is on a phone
- playwright + chrome devtools mcp for regression tests

the bugs

- sentry mcp catches the error
- agent reads the stack trace and opens a fix pr in under 10 minutes
- human just approves

the data

- posthog mcp cron at 7am on yesterday's funnel
- any step that drops more than 10%, the agent watches 20 session replays and tells me why
- stripe mcp pulls every cancellation reason into one doc every monday

the agents' tools

- orgo so every agent gets its own computer
- agentmail so every agent gets its own inbox
- agentphone so i can call them from the car
- composio connect-apps for every other connector
- akitaonrails/ai-memory, a git-backed markdown wiki so they remember what we decided last week

the skills

- wshobson/agents so skills work across claude code, codex and opencode
- my writing voice
- our design system
- how we write specs
- skill creator so the agents write new skills themselves

some helpful tricks

- one agent per platform. the x agent never touches email
- cheap model for triage, opus for anything that ships
- every output gets scored 1-10 by an llm judge. under 8 goes back
- every agent writes a 5-line log at night so i can read the whole company in 2 minutes
- every agent mistake becomes a new skill, so it only happens once

the team

- humans get version 5, not my voice note which they are happy about lol 
- their job is creative feedback, relationships and telling the agents what they got wrong

a human pm reviews the funnel once a week. this reviews it every morning

running a company is now voice notes and inference

hits.name: Ryan
hits.hook: [X article] The 𝕏 Algorithm Explained, In Depth
hits.original_en:
[X article] The 𝕏 Algorithm Explained, In Depth

How the 𝕏 algorithm (actually) works, what it rewards, and the best practices to increase your reach. Tag your @bot to digest this entire breakdown. 
Everything in today's article comes directly from the open-source code and my experience, so it's practical.
Why listen to me? 
My entire job is to hack social media algorithms. On 𝕏 in particular, I have 1B+ lifetime impressions, and I've created and pioneered many of today's viral strategies.
Including: article + QT strategy, article + GIF meta, infographic meta & many more.
Not to mention, over the past 4 weeks, I started my own brand and have already grown to 8,000+ followers and generated 4M+ impressions - purely solo (no big accounts boosting, engagement groups, etc.) 
 
With that said, I am NOT from the 𝕏 algorithm team. This is purely my interpretation of the code. 
 
This article is pretty dense. For a condensed version, I recommend screenshotting this post and watching my video below at 2x speed.
 
Your roadmap:
How to think about algorithms
The three primary 𝕏 algorithms: Thunder, Phoenix & SimClusters
The Judge: how posts get scored & weighted
The Bouncer: filters, account reputation & Under the Hood
Myths, busted
Random quirks
Practical advice 
 
How to think about algorithms
A little bit of context for how I think about social media: at the end of the day, algos are essentially games and math. Especially the 𝕏 algorithm.
An algo's entire job is to "match" content with the right demographic to keep users engaged and on the platform. At any given time, a social media algorithm pushes various content, topics, hooks, and messaging angles based on user demand and data.
When people say, "Algos don't matter, just post whatever you want!" they're fundamentally ignoring the entire reason algorithms exist.
So no, you can't just post whatever you want. It doesn't work that way. You have to reverse-engineer your content to actually get pushed.
At a high level, here's how the 𝕏 algo works:
1. The Scout: when someone opens 𝕏, three scouting algorithms go out and grab posts based on what the algorithm thinks that person might like.
2. The Judge: 𝕏 guesses what each person will do with each post (like, reply, share, follow, scroll past, mute, etc.) and gives it a weighted score.
3. The Bouncer: the highest-scoring posts get one final filter
Once a post passes all three stages, it lands on the For You page. That's where posts go really viral.
 
Now let's break down each stage:
 
The Three Primary Algorithms
𝕏 runs three algorithms. I call them the Scouts. Their job is to find posts based on what the algorithm thinks each person might like.
1. Thunder (your home base)  
Thunder pulls posts from people you follow. If you think about the way 𝕏 works, people are essentially put into little bubbles. There's a certain group of people you probably interact with on a regular basis, and that's your bubble.  When you open up your For You timeline fresh into the app, Thunder pulls posts from these people. 
2. Phoenix (where the virality lies)  
Phoenix is a very interesting algorithm, and it's where this platform's virality really lies. It's essentially an algorithm that predicts what you'll want to see before you've ever followed the person who posted it.
 3. SimClusters (your niche)  
Outside of that, you have SimClusters: posts that are popular in your niche.  SimClusters group accounts and posts by who engages with what. Basically, communities of people with shared interests.  For example, I wrote an article on my page about Head of Content, which went viral a few weeks ago. It wasn't a platform-wide viral article, but it went viral within the tech startups, marketing, and content niche. 
(Bonus: there's also a fourth, smaller source called Popular Posts, a shared list of popular recent posts, initially seeded from the most-followed active accounts.)
 
 
The Judge: How Posts Get Scored & Weighted
Once the Scouts grab posts, they hand them to what I call the Judge.  
For every post and every viewer, the Judge (Phoenix's ranking model, built on the same architecture as Grok) predicts how likely that person is to like it, reply, share it, read the whole thing, follow you, and so on.
It's essentially a gamified points and reduction system:
 
 
What this tells us:  
Shares are king (again, 𝕏 wants people on the platform).
 Conversations beat likes. Replies and quotes are weighted 7.5x more than a like. 
Likes barely move the needle. 
Negative feedback is absolutely brutal.
The adjustments: After a score is calculated, a few more things can push it up or down:  
1. Posting too much: If you post too many posts, the algorithm basically doesn't give all of them a chance to push out. 
2. Out-of-network discount: Posts from accounts you don't follow get their score multiplied by a factor below 
3. The small account boost: This is actually super cool: small accounts get a bit of a boost now.  I noticed this almost immediately. I started posting on 𝕏 about four weeks ago, and within three days I had my first viral post.
 
 
The Bouncer: Filtering & Under the Hood
So the Scouts pull posts, the Judge scores them, and the "Bouncer" filters them.  
Once a post passes all three stages, I interpret that as the highest possible chance of landing on the For You timeline.
A few categories of posts are consistently filtered out on 𝕏:
Posts older than 48 hours: 𝕏 is real-time. You generally have a 48-hour window to make a post pop.
Posts you've already seen.
Reposts and replies from people you don't follow.
Blocked accounts, muted accounts, and muted keywords. 
Spam, flagged accounts, and bots
Account reputation 
• Blocks and reports vs. likes: too many can get your account labeled. 
• Account credibility: a PageRank-style score based on who follows and engages with you. Network quality matters (not just size).
• Inauthentic behavior: 𝕏 tracks your actions over time
Under The Hood
𝕏's transparency tool shows labels limiting your account's visibility, including posts marked as spam
 
How to stay on the right side of the Bouncer:  
Don't use AI to write and post 100% of your copy. 
Get Premium, and verify your ID if you're comfortable. 
Avoid negativity and content that gets you muted, blocked or reported.
 
Myth Busters & Random Quirks Sections
Myths, busted
 "Profile clicks are a huge signal." Not anymore. Profile clicks are currently weighted at 0. Conversions are what count.  
"Likes are what matter most." A like is one of the weakest positive signals (0.66). Shares, replies, quotes, and follows matter far more.
 "Big accounts get guaranteed reach." Every account has to fight to stay relevant. I've seen many big accounts die over the last ~18 months.
Small accounts can't go viral." False. Small accounts get a built-in cold-start boost on fresh posts.
Engagement groups no longer have the same effect they once did
Random quirks 
Your feed is built from roughly 2,000+ candidates every time. 
The algorithm reads your last ~1,000 actions. Your recent engagement history (likes, replies, shares, etc.) is the main input the model uses to predict what you'll want to see.
The algorithm uses signals like your installed apps, inferred gender and location (via IP) to personalize your feed.
The weights often change. The like weight moved from 0.5 in August to 0.66 now, with no announcement.
 
Practical Advice 
1. Make content people actually want to share
Remember, the algorithm wants to keep users on the platform. Shares, replies, and quotes are the most valuable actions.
Create posts and formats that are easy to scan and share.
Spark conversation. You want people replying in your comments.
Provide real value and original insights from your experience, your network, your job. Basically, your unfair market advantages.
2. Grab attention fast
Learn how to write hooks.
Learn copywriting.
If you're mainly a video creator, invest in a proper setup (camera, mic, lighting).
3. Post original content
Never copy someone one-for-one. Credit others, and use the Post Image/Video feature that 𝕏 offers, 
Don't be reactive to what other creators are doing. Stay on the cutting edge.
4. One idea per post
If a post has multiple ideas, split it into multiple posts.
Every post needs a clear takeaway, a specific person it's for, and a specific CTA.
Mixed topics make it hard for the algorithm to know who to show it to, especially within SimClusters.
5. Avoid negativity 
I personally recommend staying away from negativity and political content.
Don't go back and forth with trolls. Block or mute them instead. Arguing risks them muting or blocking you, which suppresses your reach.
6. Build a dense network of high-quality individuals
Engage genuinely with people in your niche. It strengthens your reach and your account credibility.
7. Test every format 𝕏 is pushing
Threads, articles, media, etc. 
 
So, there you have it, the full decoding of the open-source 𝕏 algo. Note that there are obviously pieces

hits.hook: how to turn grok bot into your long-form writing machine:
hits.original_en:
how to turn grok bot into your long-form writing machine:

anything that requires good copywriting, i run it inside grok bot... agents open Opencode sessions and call Opus 5.5 and Kimi K3 on every piece (the best models for writing)

because long form is where AI usually falls apart, and it took me three fixes to get it right

step 1: control what the model sees

give it all your research and it'll use every single fact... the piece comes back dense and unreadable

so before writing, one prompt picks the few receipts the piece actually needs and hides the rest

step 2: give each model one job

every model is good at one stage and bad at the rest, so i split them:

> Kimi K3 brainstorms and simplifies... the only model i've found that dumbs ideas down
> Opus 5.5 takes it from there to the final pass

the model that starts a piece never finishes it

step 3: lock the structure

left alone, a model invents a new shape every time... so i keep a template for every part of a piece:

> how to open
> how to sequence an argument
> how to name the reader's pains
> how to close

then my Obsidian vault holds great writing broken into those same parts, one note each... so the model builds from proven parts and never copies whole pieces

your job is dumping the idea, approving the outline and doing the final edit

the value inside is still on you... no model gives you that

hits.original_en:
I constantly find myself reminding people just because AI is dropping the cost of building software to zero doesn’t mean you should default to building everything.

People are trigger happy when it comes to build vs. buy without fully considering the opportunity cost of their time & cognitive load.

My general rule of thumb is to focus build resources on 3 things:

1) Core processes or product that maintain or extend your edge. Example: for stitch fix their styling and recommendation algorithms; for an insurance co, their risk models for underwriting 

2) Owning your context. This doesn’t mean you need to own the models and it also doesn’t mean you need to own the plumbing. It means you do need to capture and organize your tribal knowledge + the eval data. 

3) Huge cost dislocations where the ROI of ripping a vendor out and replacing it with a build hits an internally assigned threshold

Compound Engineering 3.35.0 is out!

The biggest change in this release is that we've evolved what it means to compound knowledge in your repos. 

Historically, we've captured knowledge only in docs, but over the last few months we've been inching towards broadening that approach.

Now, ce-compound picks the best way to encode the learnings and prevent mistakes:

We've also combined `/ce-compound-refresh` into `/ce-compound` so there's only one skill to remember to invoke or use in automations.

Also in this one:

- `/ce-help` tells you which of the 37 skills to reach for next

- UI PRs get real before/after screenshots, inspired by @vercel's "before-and-after" skill.  Unlike there's we don't assume agent-browser, and will use what you have avaialable.

- PR babysitting is way faster, including with stacked PRs, often 60%+ faster to land.

- `/ce-debug` will still do a great job finding the root causes of your bugs/issues, but also do an even better job at implementing protection so the same class of bugs won't happen again

- `/lfg` can ship small work without a plan file. Faster and less token heavy for smaller work, letting your rip through your tasks.

hits.name: Alex Vacca
hits.hook: [X article] How to Build a GTM Engine in 2027 That Turns Signals Into Pipeline (all 4 levels)
hits.original_en:
[X article] How to Build a GTM Engine in 2027 That Turns Signals Into Pipeline (all 4 levels)

GTM (go-to-market) architecture is the way your tools, your data and your team connect into 1 system. It has 4 levels. At the bottom, a person clicks through every tab to get this week's campaign out. At the top, outbound, content and ads run on 1 account list, and the engine gets better every round.
At Frontal, we build and run outbound, signal tracking and workflows for B2B teams. The 4 levels come from what we've learned at 300+ companies and 1,000+ failed campaigns.
The bar for the top level is lower than it looks. This playbook takes you there 1 build at a time, with a 1-page cheat sheet for every level. By the end, you'll have:
→ a campaign that works by hand for 25 people before it goes to 5,000
→ a Clay workflow that scores every company before you pay for contact data
→ an email waterfall that runs the cheapest provider 1st
→ Claude skills that read 1 context file and run your tools by MCP
→ 1 account list and 1 CRM shared by outbound, content and ads
→ a test loop that judges every change on pipeline
The rule behind all 4: build the level above yours, 1 piece per quarter, and judge every piece on pipeline.
 
The 4 levels in 1 view
The 4 levels describe how much of your GTM system runs by itself, and how much still runs through someone's hands.
 
Find your team in 1 of these 4 lines:
→ Level 1: someone clicks through every step, tab by tab, and the CRM gets updated by hand as the last job of the day.
→ Level 2: a Clay workflow scores companies and finds emails the same way every time.
→ Level 3: Claude skills read 1 context file, run your tools and hand the output to a person to check.
→ Level 4: outbound, content and ads share 1 list and 1 CRM, and every result feeds the next round.
You'd never guess how many teams sit on Level 1 from the GTM bubble on LinkedIn. Your level comes from the systems you've built, and a team with an AI-powered stack can still be on Level 1. Hiring for GTM today, I'd stop counting the tools someone has used and look at the systems they've built.
Build the levels in order. Each one runs on what's been built below it.
 
Level 1: The Tool Operator (tools by hand)
Goal: get this week's campaign out.
Mindset: the tools are the job.
 
Enriching means adding data to a record, like an email or a headcount. A sequence is the series of emails each person gets.
I'd start every campaign here. It has to work by hand for 25 people before it goes to 5,000. Doing it by hand, you'll see every step, every tool and every place where the data breaks.
In the pipeline audits we run, I keep seeing teams run 1 campaign across separate tabs. Some still update the CRM by hand.
The trouble comes from staying here, with an AI-powered stack and a person who still has to click everything.
 
Step 1: Run your 1st campaign by hand for 25 people.
Find 25 companies that fit your ICP (ideal customer profile: the kind of company that looks like your best customers) and 1 buyer at each in Clay. Get each buyer's email from Prospeo, send from 1 inbox in Instantly and log every reply in the CRM you'll keep, HubSpot or Attio.
Read every reply yourself. They'll tell you whether the list, the offer and the message work before you put money behind any of them.
 
Step 2: Write down every step while you do it.
Give each step 1 line: the tool, what goes in and what comes out. You'll turn this list into your Level 2 workflow.
 
Step 3: Audit what you already pay for.
List every tool, inbox and seat. Next to each one, write who uses it and what it feeds. A head of marketing told us they had about 50 cold email mailboxes set up, and nobody was using them. This audit is where mailboxes like those show up. Cancel what nobody uses. You'll connect the rest in Step 4.
 
Step 4: Connect the stack by MCP, API or webhook.
These are the 3 ways tools pass work to each other:
→ MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets Claude use a tool directly. From 1 prompt, Claude can search companies in Clay, find an email in Prospeo and add the person to a lemlist campaign. You'll set it up in Level 3.
→ API connects 1 tool to another through code or a built-in integration. Clay's "Add Lead to Campaign" action pushes every verified person into an Instantly campaign you've already created.
→ Webhook sends data the moment something happens. Instantly's reply webhook, or its CRM sync, logs each reply in your CRM. Both need Instantly's Hypergrowth plan.
 
How to improve:
❌ Stop running 1 campaign across separate tabs.
✅ Connect the stack by MCP, API or webhook.
Level 1 checkpoint: 1 campaign that worked by hand for 25 people, every step written down and your tools connected to each other.
 
 
Level 2: The Workflow Builder (workflows)
Goal: steps that run the same way every time.
Mindset: every step is a function with 1 job.
 
A function takes 1 input, does 1 job and hands 1 output to the next step. A broken step is easy to find: each job lives in 1 step.
We've built this level in Clay.
Step 1: Pull your companies into a Clay table.
Use your ICP filters to pull companies into a Clay table. Enrich each one with its industry, headcount and tech stack.
 
Step 2: Track signals and triggers on every company.
We track 70 signals and 37 triggers in Clay.
→ A signal is a fact that makes a company likelier to buy: the team it's hiring for, the tools it runs, how fast its headcount grows.
→ A trigger is a dated event that starts the workflow: a new funding round, a new leader in the team you sell to, a job post that names your category.
In Clay, turn on "Monitor for news & fundraising", "Monitor for new hire" and "Monitor for job changes" (Signals start on Clay's Launch plan). Add columns for job posts and tech stack. Pick the signals that showed up most in your closed-won deals (the deals you won) 1st. You'll add more as the workflow proves itself.
 
Step 3: Score the company.
Give each fit rule and each signal a number of points. Add them up in a Clay formula column and write the cutoff down.
 
The signal goes in the score and stays out of the email. The message talks about the company's situation.
 
Step 4: Put the fit gate in front of your data spend.
Every people, email and phone lookup costs credits. Add Clay's people search with the job titles of your persona (the role you sell to) to find 1 buyer per company. Open its Run Settings and add an "Only run if" condition: the score is at or above your cutoff. Give every email and phone column the same condition. Clay won't run these lookups on any company under the cutoff.
 
Step 5: Hold the companies that fail the gate.
Tag them "held" and keep them in their own view. Re-score them when their facts change: a funding round, a new hire on the buying team, a new tool in their stack. Each month, re-run the signal columns on the held view, and the score formula updates with them. A company that's failing today can pass next quarter.
 
Step 6: Run the email waterfall, cheapest provider 1st.
A waterfall asks 1 provider for the email, then passes every miss to the next one. Ours runs in this order:
 
In Clay, add a 2nd condition to each provider's column, next to the score cutoff: the column before it came back empty. Clay bills every step that returns data. That's why the cheapest provider goes 1st.
Across 1,000+ lists, the waterfall finds 85 to 90% of emails.
 
Step 7: Send from Instantly.
Create 1 Instantly campaign per persona before this step. Clay pushes each verified person into the campaign for their persona, Instantly sends, and every reply lands in your CRM (Level 1, Step 4).
 
Step 8: Read a sample of the rejects.
Someone on the team reads a sample of the companies your score threw out. For every good account in that pile, they'll change the rule that cut it.
 
How to improve:
❌ Stop paying for email and phone data before the person passes the fit score.
✅ Hold the companies that don't fit. Re-score them when their facts change.
Level 2 checkpoint: every company scored, contact data bought past the fit gate, a 3-provider waterfall and a regular read of the rejects.
 
 
Level 3: The Context Engineer (skills + context)
Goal: output that follows your playbook.
Mindset: write the context once. Every skill reads it.
 
A Claude skill works like an onboarding doc for a new hire. It tells Claude to read 1 file with your ICP, personas, offers and rules, then run Clay, Prospeo and lemlist by MCP.
Ivan Falco, our Head of ABM, runs $200K+ a month in client ad spend through 12 Claude Code skills.
Claude Code is Anthropic's AI agent that runs in your terminal. Make a project folder and open Claude Code inside it. Every file below lives in that folder.
 
Step 1: Write 1 context file.
Save it as context.md in your project folder. Every skill reads this file before it does anything, so you'll update it the day your ICP or your offer changes.
 
 
Step 2: Write your 1st skill.
In Claude Code, a skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file inside. The top of the file holds its name and a description of when to use it, and the body holds the steps. Save the folder in .claude/skills/ inside your project. Claude picks the skill up whenever a task matches its description. It's a plain text file anyone on the team can edit.
 
 
Step 3: Connect the tools by MCP.
→ Clay: connect it from Claude's connector directory. Clay says it works in Claude Code too. It runs Clay's company and contact search plus the Functions your workspace admin turns on. It can't browse your tables.
→ Prospeo: its MCP server needs Node.js 18+ and your Prospeo API key. It'll return verified emails and mobile numbers.
 
→ lemlist: add it with the command below, then run /mcp in Claude Code and log in. It'll ask you to confirm before anything that sends, deletes, spends credits or changes a campaign.
 
 
Step 4: Run every skill on 10/80/10.
My rule for AI is 10/80/10. A person decides the task, the skill does 80% of the work, and a person checks the last 10% before anything goes out.
 
Step 5: Turn the calls you make by feel into skills.
Write down the decisions your team makes on instinct every week. What to test next is a good 1st one, and it's the one we'd pick. A next-test skill reads last round's results from a CRM export, finds the weakest part (the companies, the persona or the copy) and proposes 1 change for the next round.
 
How to improve:
❌ Stop rewriting the copy when replies drop. It might be the last thing that's broken.
✅ Turn the calls you make by feel, like what to test next, into skills.

[X article] Claude 2.0: Everything That's Changed (FULL GUIDE)

Claude 2.0 is here, and it's incredible.
Claude has changed more in the last few weeks than most people realize.
Here's everything worth knowing (including prompts to test yourself). 
 
I. Giving Claude a Team of "Helpers"
You can now equip Claude with a team of "helper" subagents that pop up in sidechats. 
Instead of researching, writing, and planning in separate chats, you give Claude the main job and let its helpers work on different parts in parallel. The main conversation collects their work when they're done.
Let's say you're launching a $49 digital product. You need competitor research, X posts, and a sales page. Rather than prompting for all three one after another, try this:
 
Prompt:
 
You can follow each helper's progress from the task panel where the feature is available.
For a larger ongoing project, Claude Code can also work with an approved repository of source files. That prevents every helper from working with a different version of the facts.
 
 
II.  Manage Your Other Sessions in One Chat

hits.name: Alex Lieberman
hits.hook: There's a major cyberattack happening weekly, and every exec is scrambling to make sure they're not the next victim.
hits.original_en:
There's a major cyberattack happening weekly, and every exec is scrambling to make sure they're not the next victim. 

I sat down with David Campbell (@dcam_ai), former head of security research at Scale AI, who has advised dozens of governments and enterprises on cyber.

Complete list of notes (and link to full convo) below...

Big takeaways:
- Security has gone through three chapters: castle and moat (about 30 years), cloud (about 10 years) and now AI (about 4 years).
- Early AI security over-focused on model behavior and guardrails, while people handed agents their credentials.
- "The next 18-to-24 months are going to be hell for cybersecurity professionals," largely because they're bringing a knife to a gun fight. 
- His advice for the next 18 months: go back to a hard exterior and protect yourself at the edge.

The three eras:
- Castle and moat: "A really hard exterior and then a soft squishy interior." Companies ran their own hardware and focused limited people on external threats, mostly fraud.
- Writing an exploit meant picking a target, scanning it and writing custom software, so the barrier to entry was extremely high.
- Cloud: AWS, GCP and Azure standardized everyone's ingress so leverage was given to attackers. "If this worked on company A, let me see if it also works on company B, C, D." 
- A wave of cyber-educated grads, script kiddies running code they didn't understand, and app-layer bugs led to the rise of bug bounties.

Cyber at Uber and DoorDash:
- He was about engineer 200 at Uber and there were about 4,000 when he left. Uber built its own bot detection before Cloudflare offered it.
- Uber's rule: "If you do something once, it better be scriptable and repeatable."
- A multi-cloud provisioning tool took six people eight months. "I'm pretty sure I could probably build it myself in a weekend now with an LLM."
- DoorDash had under 1,000 engineers, leaned on mature open source like Cloudflare, Envoy and HashiCorp, and blended roles. "DoorDash was able to do more with less."

How a security org is structured:
- The CISO reports to the CEO, or to legal or engineering depending on the company. Then within security you have: 
1) Cloud security: infrastructure security (IAM policies, access control lists) plus product security (engineers who build securely).
2) Security operations: the SOC, forensics and incident command. Red teams usually live here as the org matures.
3) GRC: legal and regulatory compliance.

Failure mode in AI security: 
- People treated the model as a new way into the application instead of one part of the system. "Models should never control deterministic systems like this."
- Asking a model "please don't release this password" is "completely backwards."
- "If I could convince your model to build a pipe bomb, that may be embarrassing, but it's not an incident."

BICO framework for agents: 
Behavior: what the system chooses to do
- What instructions, retrieved context, memories, or tool outputs can influence its decisions? Can it distinguish data from instructions? Are important actions validated independently of the model that proposed them?

Identity: who is acting, and under what authority
- Is the agent distinguishable from the human who initiated the task? Are its credentials short-lived and scoped to this specific job, or does it inherit a service account that can act across customers, repositories, or environments?

Control: where reasoning ends and authorization begins
- Control asks which deterministic boundaries the environment enforces between reasoning and action. Which tools, parameters, data, and destinations are permitted? When must an action cross a policy check or approval gate?

Observability: whether the decision chain can be reconstructed
- Observability asks whether defenders can reconstruct the decision chain. That means recording the relevant context sources, identity and authorization events, tools invoked, policies evaluated, approvals granted, changes made, and final outcome.

Why defenders are losing:
- David's ICLR paper on "defensive refusal bias" gave student blue teamers an LLM during the NCCDC competition. When they said it was for security work, they got refused 2.7x more than when they just asked "Is this malware?"
- "We may have overtrained our models to not be as helpful for cybersecurity defenders."
- "Right now it's a huge unfair advantage. The bad guys are moving exponentially faster."

Why every company is a target:
- Attacks went from 6 to 8 months to build one targeted worm, to one exploit sprayed across the cloud, to machine speed.
- Nation-state attackers can now target a water treatment plant and also "literally every single company that they have access to."
- Big companies will be fine. He worries about "the mortgage bank that has one IT person."

What to do right now:
- Harden the edge and triage vulnerabilities as fast as you can.
- Hire more security people until models can actually help defenders.
- Build engineering tools, and swap AI guardrails for controls that are "as deterministic as possible."
- Expect burnout on security teams in the coming months.

Which AI leader should I speak with next? 

Full interview with David: https://t.co/sGCnWCCs4b

hits.original_en:
This might sound weird coming from a "guy making content" because I should sell you difficult setups, but the best Claude setup is no setup:

Let's start with-

> Not using Claude with a personal account.
> Not using Claude without its desktop app.
> Not using Claude without trying Claude Code.

Then the actual setup of your Claude:

(mind you, delete this setup again in 5 months)

1. Check that you have one Claude.

Go to Claude Settings → Organization Settings → Capabilities.

2. Pick 'Auto' in Claude Chat.

In the message box, switch Manual to Auto. Claude works without stopping to ask you at every step.

Default: Opus 5.5 + High + Auto.

3. Claude Chat writes code.

Everything is code. A slide. An image. A video. 

So when Claude can write code, it builds the thing instead of describing it.

Now, go to the left menu bar in Claude. Pick Design.

Pick Slides. Write a prompt of what you want exactly. Prompt it until you like what you see. You can upload references too.

4. Delete your old Claude setup.

> Account → “Instructions for Claude." Empty.
> Claude Customize → Skills. Remove.
> Skills → Yours → Search “writing” → Turn off.
> Claude Settings → Memory → Turn it off.
> Any over-organised folder you maintain.
> Delete global instructions. It ignores it anyway.

5. One clear goal.

Prompting is sharing your goal. Claude figures out the how. It can’t guess what you want (and why).

Start all the new chats with this prompt template:

"Goal: [what you want, and what it's for] Context: [who it's for, what you already have, what good looks like] Before you start, restate in your own words what you think my goals are and the problem I'm trying to solve. If you need more context, ask me questions."

6. Ask for HTML page.

Stop asking for a Word file, a PowerPoint or a PDF. 

Try asking for an HTML. Claude builds it as an Artifact: a web page that lives in your Claude account. 

Add this to your prompt:

"Make it an HTML page."

7. Switch from your old folders.

Open the Claude desktop app & select your old folder (mine was called CLAUDE COWORK). It’s the last time Claude reads it.

hits.hook: n8n runs more than 12,000 automated workflows inside its own company.
hits.original_en:
n8n runs more than 12,000 automated workflows inside its own company.

Its new product lets AI agents run workflows like those, exactly as they were built.

The product is n8n Agents, and @n8n_io has now launched it.

An agent works toward a goal and decides its own steps. That is what makes it useful, and also what makes it hard to trust with real work. When an agent sends the wrong email or issues the wrong refund, there is usually no clear record of why.

n8n's answer is to let the agent call workflows as tools. The agent still reads the request and decides what needs to happen. But when it reaches a step that matters, such as a refund, an invoice or a change to a customer record, it hands that step to a workflow the team already built, and the workflow runs exactly as written. Every step is logged, and sensitive actions can require a person's approval before they go through.

Most of the industry is pushing toward agents that do everything on their own. n8n is betting that companies want judgment from the model and execution from a process they already trust.

The catch is that an agent built this way is only as good as the workflows behind it. If your processes aren't written down yet, n8n is where you build them first, then hand them to an agent.

For a company already running 12,000 workflows, that work is done. Years of process become something an agent can call instead of improvise.

[X article] How to Master System Design for Building with AI (Full Course)

I'm going to show you how to make an AI agent think in system design before it writes code.
because the agent already types faster than you. what it lacks is a set of decisions about where data lives, what happens under load, and what happens when a part fails.
those decisions are system design.
if the decisions live only in your head, the agent guesses. if they live in a file and in tests, the agent can check its own work against them.
that's the whole move... turn each concept into a rule the agent reads and a test the agent must fail once on purpose.
these are the system design concepts an agent must think through. each one is something your agent must reason about, write down, and check.
one note before the plan.
every number in a worked example is illustrative unless a source is linked.
every test outcome is an expected outcome, not a result i measured.
here's the plan:
why prompting alone does not hold a design
how to approach a design
performance vs scalability
latency vs throughput
availability vs consistency
DNS, CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy
the application layer
the database
the cache
background jobs and retries
communication
security basics the agent must not skip
how to encode all of it for an agent
worked design: a feed, with and without the concepts
real systems as reference cards
where this method breaks
your first week
the law
 
why prompting alone does not hold a design
an agent solves the request in front of it.
ask for a feed and you get a feed. it works for one user on one laptop with one database and no failures.
the gaps appear later:
a webhook arrives twice
a second server starts
a dependency hangs for thirty seconds
someone needs a restore
none of that was in the request, so none of it is in the code.
a prompt cannot fix this alone.
the agent reads a prompt once. the next session starts without it.
three things persist between sessions:
SYSTEM.md holds the design decisions and the numbers behind them
MODULES.md holds one contract per module: what it owns, what it promises, how it fails
red tests hold the checks, and they run in continuous integration (CI), which runs every check on each proposed change
a red test is a test that you make fail on purpose once.
you inject the fault it targets and watch it go red. then you fix the code and watch it go green.
this step matters.
a new test that never failed has not shown that it can see its fault.
so the rule for the whole article is simple:
before you trust a new test, make it fail for the fault it is meant to catch.
keep the claim narrow.
this method gives you a concrete way to review the agent's work.
the tests catch the failures you define. they do not catch the failures you forget.
research on agent context files is also mixed:
one 2026 study measured runtime and tokens. correctness was not its main measure (https://arxiv.org/html/2601.20404)
another found context files tend to reduce task success and increase inference cost by over 20% (https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988)
a third found no measurable correctness gain across its runs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27250)
that is why the file alone is not the method.
the file guides the agent. the tests check the behavior.
every concept below gets the same treatment: plain meaning, the decision the agent must make, a SYSTEM.md rule, and a red test.
 
how to approach a design
i use four steps. they work for an agent as well as for a person.
outline use cases, constraints, and assumptions
create a high level design with the main components
design the core components in detail
scale the design by finding and fixing bottlenecks
the failure to watch for is a start at step 3. the agent picks a framework and writes handlers before it knows who uses the system.
so make step 1 a written artifact. the agent answers these questions in SYSTEM.md before it writes code:
who uses it?
how do they use it?
how many users are there?
what does the system do?
what are the inputs and outputs?
how much data do we expect?
how many requests per second (RPS) do we expect?
what is the read to write ratio?
the agent may not know many of these answers. that is fine.
it must label each one.
MEASURED means you have data for it
TARGET means you chose it as a goal
GUESS means nobody knows yet
a GUESS is honest. a number with no label is a hidden guess.
back-of-the-envelope math
back-of-the-envelope math is a rough estimate done by hand. it tells you which problems are real at your size.
here is my conversion guide. it is easy to remember:
a month has about 2.5 million seconds
1 request per second is about 2.5 million requests per month
40 requests per second is about 100 million requests per month
400 requests per second is about 1 billion requests per month
here it is on a paste site:
10 million paste writes per month is about 4 writes per second
100 million reads per month is about 40 reads per second
it also sizes storage.
at about 1.27 KB per paste, 10 million pastes a month is about 12.7 GB of new content per month. over three years that is about 450 GB.
those are assumptions, not measurements.
the method is the point.
for sizes, think in powers of two:
2^10 is about a thousand (1 KB)
2^20 is about a million (1 MB)
2^30 is about a billion (1 GB)
2^40 is about a trillion (1 TB)
an estimate only needs the right order of magnitude.
traffic is not even across the day. peak traffic is higher than the average.
choose a peak factor from your traffic data. until you have data, mark the factor GUESS.
concurrency is not a pool size
Little's law connects three numbers. the average number of requests in flight equals the arrival rate times the average time each request spends in the system.
so 1,000 requests per second at 200 ms each gives 200 requests in flight on average.
that is the concurrency your design must support. it is not your connection pool size.
to size a pool, the agent must do more work:
divide the concurrency across the instances you run
find where requests wait (database, model API, disk, lock)
add headroom for bursts above the average
load-test the limit and record the result as MEASURED
here is the intake prompt. paste it before any build.
 
to practice the intake, run it on designs you already know:
a paste site
a timeline
a web crawler
a personal finance tracker
a social graph
a key-value cache for search
a sales rank by category
a web app that grows to millions of users
 
performance vs scalability
here is the split.
a performance problem means the system is slow for a single user.
a scalability problem means the system is fast for a single user but slow under heavy load.
a service is scalable if added resources give a proportional increase in performance.
the agent must classify a slow complaint before it fixes anything. the fixes are different.
a quadratic loop is a performance problem. more servers do not fix it.
a single in-process lock is a scalability problem. a faster query does not fix it.
the rule for SYSTEM.md:
 
the red test:
 
 
latency vs throughput
latency is the time to perform one action.
throughput is the number of actions per unit of time.
aim for maximal throughput with acceptable latency. the agent must define "acceptable" as a number.
published tables of latency numbers help with orders of magnitude. memory is faster than disk, and a call inside one data center is faster than a call across regions.
treat those tables as historical rules of thumb. the agent measures its own system and labels the result MEASURED.
averages hide the slow tail. so use percentiles.
p50 means 50% of requests finish at or below this latency. p99 means 99% of requests finish at or below this latency.
tail latency grows when one request waits on many calls. the request is only as fast as its slowest dependency.
the failure to watch for is an external call with no timeout. one hung dependency then holds a worker until the worker pool is empty.
the rule:

availability vs consistency
this is the CAP theorem. CAP stands for consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
here are the terms:
consistency means every read receives the most recent write or an error
availability means every request receives a response, which may not hold the most recent write
partition tolerance means the system keeps working when the network splits its parts
networks fail, so a distributed system must tolerate partitions. during a partition, it must choose between consistency and availability.
CP means the system picks consistency during a partition.
some requests time out or return errors. it fits data that needs atomic reads and writes.
AP means the system picks availability during a partition.
reads can return stale data. it fits data that can be eventually consistent.
the agent must make this choice per data type, not per system. one app holds both kinds.
here is how i would sort a typical product. these are my defaults, not a law.
money, plan status, permissions, inventory: consistent
like counts, view counts, follower counts, feed order: can be eventual
consistency patterns
i use three patterns.
weak consistency: after a write, reads may or may not see it. examples are memcached and realtime uses such as voice calls and games.
eventual consistency: after a write, reads see it after a delay. data is copied asynchronously. examples are DNS and email.
strong consistency: after a write, reads see it. data is copied synchronously. examples are file systems and relational databases.
the failure to watch for here is read-your-writes. a user posts, the app reads from a replica that lags, and the new post is missing.
replicas lag. the delay can grow under load or failure.

availability patterns
there are two complementary patterns: failover and replication.
failover moves traffic to a standby when the active server fails.
active-passive: the active and passive servers exchange heartbeats. if the heartbeat stops, the passive server takes over. downtime depends on whether the standby is hot (running) or cold (must start).
active-active: both servers take traffic and share the load.
failover has costs. it adds hardware and complexity.
data can be lost if the active server fails before new writes reach the standby.
replication keeps copies of data on more than one server. the database section covers it.

2. Write Posts in the 4 Formats That Get Saved

The opportunity: "You could pull $X a month doing Y for Z." The $20k-a-month penny stock websites post above: 2,235 bookmarks. A post about a guide on how to do a handstand making $80,000 a month: 783.

The tool setup: the tool, then steps they can follow today. A walkthrough of GPT Sol and Astra for browser work: 1,778 bookmarks.
The big-number explainer: a figure people can't picture, made concrete. My post that measured billionaire spending in Ferraris (a mega yacht is 1,400 of them) hit 455,983 views.
Don't chase views for this. My most-viewed post of the past year was a story about a tuk tuk driver in Cambodia asking if I wanted to go shoot guns.
 
558,865 views. Only 644 bookmarks.
The penny stock websites post got more than three times the saves on a sixth of the views. The saves come from posts that teach something, and the people who save a post are the ones who give you an email.
The receipt is the easiest one to start with, because you only need something you actually did. My "10 hours of work" post was a favor for a friend. Her coaching business had 12k+ Instagram followers and no email list at all, and in about a day I had Claude write 20 newsletters in her voice.
Stage 2 of the agent picks the format for each topic and drafts two posts in your voice, ending on a line that makes people want the detailed version.
3. Build Only for the Posts That Take Off
Writing a guide, a page and three emails for every post would eat your week.
So the agent waits. It checks each post you publish at 1, 3 and 6 hours and compares it to your own median.
When a post is pulling more bookmarks per 1,000 views than your median, you get a message with the link, its numbers and a guide idea.
You reply "go" or ignore it. Nothing gets built until you say so.
A post that takes off gets the full funnel while people are still finding it. The rest never cost you anything beyond writing them.
Stages 3 and 4 of the agent do this. The alert looks like this (example output):
 
4. One "Go" Builds the Whole Funnel
The "10 hours of work" post is the one that brought in the 113 subscribers. I had no page and no guide for it when it went up:
 
Two hours and 25 minutes after it went up, I replied to it with one line and a link:
"Want a more detailed breakdown of how I added that $50k+ in 10 hours / Check it out here"
The reply got 6,047 views, and Kit tagged every signup from it as "ai infrastructure playbook":
[IMAGE: Kit 113 tag screenshot]
That's one new subscriber for every 54 people who saw it. Run the same math on a reply with 500 views and that's about 9 new subscribers.
I built the guide and the landing page after the post started taking off. The agent does the same for every post of yours that takes off.
When you reply "go", stage 5 of the agent builds all of it in one run:
The free guide: the post expanded, with the top questions from the replies answered.
The landing page: one screen, the post's first line as the headline, its own Kit tag.
The email flow: the guide right away, the best idea from it on day 2, a real story on day 4.
The tags: a "What brings you here today?" question on the thank-you page, with exploring, starting a business and running one as Kit tags.
The plug reply: three drafts for you to pick from and post.
You read it, fix what's off, publish the page and post the reply yourself.
I once ran a 40k list split into 200+ segments. That only works if you tag people from the first day, which is why the tags come in the same run.
The plug reply doesn't have to be clever. Under a post about Lego x Pokemon sets, well outside my usual topics, I wrote "Wrote up a quick breakdown on the math behind this play (and 3 other sets with similar ROI potential)".
That reply pulled 180,389 views on its own:
 
[JAMES: second proof. Another post where a plug reply sent people to a page with its own Kit tag, and how many subscribers that tag has.]
5. The Full Agent: Paste This and Run It
This is the whole thing in one prompt. It scans and drafts on Monday, watches every post you publish, pings you when one takes off, and builds the full funnel after your "go".
It never posts anything. Every draft waits for you.
 
In Claude Code, save it as a skill and fill in the brackets.
6. Run It in Grok Bot
I'd run it in Grok Bot, since it can read X and run on a schedule without you opening it.
Connect X and paste in your Kit API key. That's how I connect mine, and it lets the agent create tags and draft emails in your account.
Paste the agent into a chat and fill in the brackets.
Make it a routine: "Run stages 1 and 2 every Monday at 8am, check each new post at 1, 3 and 6 hours, message me when one takes off, and send the stage 6 report every Friday."
On Monday you edit drafts and post. When a post takes off, you get a ping, reply "go", and approve what comes back.

one "go" builds the guide, page, emails and tags for the winners only

Korean melodrama made with using Seedance 2.5

Prompt: Create a 30-second, 1080p ultra-realistic Korean melodrama scene inside a luxurious rooftop restaurant terrace at night, overlooking the glittering city skyline. Use the uploaded reference images for exact character identity and appearance. Maintain perfect facial consistency, hairstyles, outfits, body proportions, and realistic expressions throughout the entire sequence.

MAIN CHARACTERS

Woman: Beautiful young adult Korean woman in her early 20s, long silky black hair, fitted pastel-pink crop top, stylish high-waisted mini skirt, fashionable knee-high boots, carrying an elegant shoulder handbag. Natural makeup, expressive eyes and realistic skin texture.

Boyfriend: Handsome young Korean man in his early 20s, short black hair, wearing a black fitted shirt, dark trousers and fashionable sneakers.

Other Woman: Attractive young Korean woman with long brown hair, wearing an elegant fitted white dress and heels.

— THE SHOCKING DISCOVERY

The glass doors of the rooftop terrace slowly slide open.

The young woman steps out cheerfully, holding a small gift box and her smartphone. She is about to surprise her boyfriend on their anniversary night.

But the moment she scans the candle-lit tables, she suddenly freezes.

At a secluded corner table beneath hanging string lights, her boyfriend is tenderly holding another woman's hands, then leaning in to share a lingering kiss, completely unaware that someone is watching.

Her smile instantly disappears.

Her eyes widen. She stares at them in disbelief, struggling to process what she has just witnessed.

The gift box slowly slips from her fingers and lands softly on the floor. Her eyes immediately fill with tears.

She whispers in a broken voice:

"Is this why you cancelled our dinner?"

— THE CONFRONTATION

She walks across the terrace, her heels-less boots striking the floor with determined steps, her face filled with anger and heartbreak.

Her boyfriend notices her shadow and immediately pulls away from the other woman.

He jumps up from his chair, looking completely shocked.

She says, her voice trembling:

"Happy anniversary, right? Is this the surprise you planned for me?"

He nervously responds:

"Wait, please! Let me explain, it's not what it looks like!"

She interrupts him, tears already streaming down her cheeks:

"Then tell me what it looks like! I watched you kiss her!"

The other woman looks uncomfortable, lowers her gaze and quietly steps back from the table, avoiding eye contact.

The boyfriend desperately attempts to explain, but she keeps speaking through her sobs:

"How long has this been going on? I gave you everything, and you lied to my face every single day!"

Her voice cracks, and she starts crying uncontrollably.

— THE SPLASH AND EMOTIONAL OUTBURST

He steps closer and reaches out to touch her shoulders.

She immediately shakes his hands off.

In a sudden emotional reaction, she grabs the glass of red wine from the table and throws it straight into his face.

The glass shatters on the floor, and the sound echoes across the quiet terrace.

He closes his eyes, wine dripping down his black shirt, and freezes in shock.

She breaks down completely. Tears burst out of her eyes as she struggles to catch her breath.

She cries out through her tears:

"I BELIEVED IN YOU! YOU TURNED OUR LOVE INTO A JOKE!"

She looks toward the other woman and then back at him.

"You two deserve each other!"

Her hands are shaking. Her voice becomes increasingly emotional.

— THE RING AND WALKING AWAY

She slips the silver couple ring from her finger and suddenly throws it at her boyfriend in anger. The ring bounces off his chest and rolls across the terrace floor, spinning to a stop near his sneakers.

He stands speechless, unable to react.

She wipes her tears angrily and says one final time, her voice low and trembling:

"DON'T EVER CALL MY NAME AGAIN!"

She turns toward the glass doors and quickly walks away.

Her boyfriend rushes after her, calling:

"Please! Don't leave like this, just listen to me!"

She refuses to look back.

She walks away crying, covering her mouth with one hand while her shoulders shake from sobbing.

FINAL SHOT: The camera captures a dramatic close-up of her tear-covered face as she walks through the restaurant's softly lit hallway. Her mascara is slightly smudged, her breathing is uneven, and tears continue rolling down her cheeks. Behind her, through the glass doors, her boyfriend stands helplessly on the terrace, wine-stained and alone, the other woman silently watching from the shadows.

hits.hook: Nobody has ever explained all of Claude to you.
hits.original_en:
Nobody has ever explained all of Claude to you.

But here's everything about Claude you must know:

Level 1. Don't be lazy, use the Claude desktop app.

You will still use the browser 90% of the time, and that's fine. But the day you start using the Claude desktop app, you'd be able to work with your folders without ever uploading the files one by one. You'd use Claude code more. There is no coming back from there.

Level 2. You have better things to do than spending 1 minute choosing the best model.

Default should be: Opus 5.5 on high. That's it.

Do not switch the models mid-chat. It consumes more tokens because Claude re-reads the entire chat (again) to get the context.

Level 3. Either Medium or High effort. Nothing else

Medium when it is low-effort work. High for most of the tasks. But Extra High mostly burn through your usage limit.

Level 4. Delete your old Claude setup.

Delete the “Instructions for Claude” box in settings. Delete the old added Claude skills. Old skills and prompts might be slowing you down since they were written for old models. Instead, give one goal and end prompts with: “Before you start, restate my goal in your own words.”

Level 5. Ask for HTML. Not for a document.

Add two things to your prompt: “Make it an HTML page” and “for [who will read it].”

Claude will code the image, doc, or any other format. There is no scope of making mistakes.

Level 6. Protect what you plug in.

Never click the thumbs up or down under an answer. You are basically giving feedback to AI, and they are allowed to send it to their training data. On a Team plan, once memory is on, leave it on: if an owner turns it off, every member’s memories are deleted permanently.

Your first 20 minutes, in order:

1. Install desktop app.
2. No settings are the best.
3. Connect ONE tool - not everything.
4. Use Claude Code more than you do.
5. Delete the installed skills, and add the new ones (written for the latest models)
6. Go to https://t.co/cn6xDN1uAS for my Claude skill library.

Norway now has more than 2,000 underwater AI laser robots shooting lice off its salmon

they're made by a company called Stingray, and they already guard more than 50 million salmon and trout 24/7

the reason is sea lice, tiny parasites that latch onto salmon and feed on them

as few as 11 can kill a small fish, and one pen can hold 150,000 salmon

the usual fix is pumping the fish out and blasting them with warm water or water jets to knock the lice off

but the handling is so rough that Norway's fish health report ranks it the top cause of death in full-grown farmed salmon

so instead, Stingray puts a robot inside the pen that hunts lice one at a time, all day:

> two cameras watch every salmon that swims past

> AI checks two frames to make sure it's really a louse

> then a green laser fires from up to 2 meters away

> the salmon's scales reflect the beam, so the fish swims off fine and the louse is dead

we now live in a world where AI lasers do pest control on your dinner lmao

hits.name: Alex Lieberman
hits.hook: Hot take: it’s gonna take 10+ years for AI to diffuse through most enterprises.
hits.original_en:
Hot take: it’s gonna take 10+ years for AI to diffuse through most enterprises.

Accelerationists argue “things will be different this time” and “AI will fully diffuse wayyy faster,” but the more time I spend in the guts of big companies, the more I think their view shows a fundamental misunderstanding of corporate bureaucracy and inertia.

An enterprise’s ability to metabolize raw intelligence is limited by the slowest step of what I call the Corporate SDLC. 

It goes something like this…

1. A senior sponsor (CEO, CAIO, CIO, CFO) decides it’s in their best interest to champion AI transformation. 
2. Orgwide and function-specific AI audits are done in order to map problems/opportunities to key goals.
3. AI roadmap is built based on the org readiness of initiatives uncovered during the audit. Readiness includes: ROI case, data hygiene, data access, cultural openness, define champion, process/product understanding, pilot construct & go/no go criteria, security/legal considerations.
4. Leg work (inclusive of actual work & internal politicking) done to get first initiative to pilot readiness. 
5. Build process done by internal FDEs or external partner. Includes connecting to data sources, setting up agent-based access control, doing all necessary agent infra, harness engineering, embedding business logic, setting up evals, etc. 
6. Set up pilot with proper benchmarks and change management.
7. Make scale, cut (return to step 3), or change (return to step 5) decision on pilot.
8. Complete production readiness checklist. 
9. Additional FDE & enablement work as needed. 
10. Agent deployed to production. 
11. Ongoing maintenance and progressive permissioning to the agent as it proves itself. 

If you thought optimizing & agentifying a traditional software development life cycle was cumbersome, buckle up for the enterprise version. 

There are literally thousands of ways that the corporate SDLC can be interrupted and slowed.

Stakeholder that initially agrees to initiative gets cold feet upon employee push back.
Audits with full workflow inventory and KPI base lining takes a quarter.
Data is nowhere near semantic ready for agents.
Senior sponsor finds a new job.
Access gateway doesn’t exist.

The potential friction list is endless. 

This is why the diffusion gap (distance between raw intelligence & enterprise results) is massive & only growing and why we’re in inning 1 of a decadeslong transformation arc. 

Btw, if you want help closing the diffusion gap and driving ai transformation in your company, head to tenex[.]co.

Prompt: Create a 30-second, 1080p ultra-realistic personal home-video of a naturally pretty young Korean woman in her early 20s, with straight black hair in two loose low pigtails, wearing a thick red knit beanie, a cream puffer jacket, a gray wool scarf, dark jeans, and brown winter boots. She carries a paper cup of hot cocoa.

Start immediately with her stepping out of her front door into fresh snowfall. She pulls her scarf up, turns to the camera, smiles, and says, "It snowed overnight!" She walks down a quiet residential street, boots crunching in untouched snow. Partway down, she glances at the person holding the camera, laughs, and says, "Stop filming me, it's so early!" She holds her cocoa toward the lens like a toast.

She stops at a parked car, wipes snow off the side mirror with her glove, and writes a small heart on the frosted window. Then she pauses. For about three seconds she stands still, looking up at the falling snow, breath steaming, a soft smile on her face, with only quiet ambience. The camera lingers on her.

She scoops a handful of snow, packs it into a ball, and tosses it at a bare tree. It misses, and she pouts at the camera. She tries again and hits the trunk, and a clump of snow drops from a branch onto her head. She shrieks, shakes it off, laughs, and says, "Okay, I deserved that!"

As she turns back toward home, she notices a single small red mitten sitting on a fence post. She picks it up, looks at it, then at the camera, and says, "Wait... whose is this?" She sets it back carefully on the post.

Finally, at her gate, she turns to the camera with red cheeks and a runny nose, sniffs, waves, and says, "Okay, see you! Bye!" She goes inside, and the recording abruptly cuts to black.

**Visual style:** Raw early-2000s handheld DV camcorder footage, soft overcast winter morning light, slightly overexposed snow, imperfect framing, camera shake, autofocus hunting on falling snowflakes, faded cool-toned colors, mild digital noise, a brief fogged lens when she steps outside, and realistic movements.

**Audio:** Muffled snowy neighborhood ambience, soft wind, crunching footsteps, a distant dog barking, a faint camera-holder chuckle off-screen, and perfectly synchronized casual English dialogue. No background music.

Maintain identical facial features, clothing, hairstyle, and body proportions throughout. Keep every interaction and object physically realistic.

hits.original_en:
there's one trap in AI that's costing people months of their life...

AI is insanely good at bringing ideas to life

shower thought -> market research -> full offer -> landing page

you can do all of this in a single day... but the problem is, AI will never tell you your idea sucks

so you spend weeks building... then your launch fails

because AI can't tell you:
>your ICP doesn't actually have this problem
>they have the problem but won't pay to solve it
>70 other people already tried this and failed
>your positioning makes no sense to real humans

AI is trained to be helpful and encouraging... not brutally honest about market reality

the faster AI helps you build, the easier it is to build the wrong thing

you can waste months on a fully-built product nobody wants

do this instead: build the idea in a day with AI (landing page, offer, positioning)... then immediately test it with real humans

not AI's opinion, real wallet-opening humans

- run ads to the landing page
- send cold outreach
- post about it and see who responds
- talk to 10 people in your target market

if they don't care, kill it fast

use AI to move fast & use humans to move in the right direction

hits.hook: I can't believe my Claude saved me $10,200/year (without accessing my bank account or money) with this copy-paste prompt:
hits.original_en:
I can't believe my Claude saved me $10,200/year (without accessing my bank account or money) with this copy-paste prompt:

But before blindly doing it.

→ Start by reading this: https://t.co/38nzKYzEFG.

→ Go to all your bank accounts apps.
→ Download 12 months of transactions as CSV files.
→ Put the CSV files in a folder on your desktop.
→ Go to Claude. Set it to Opus 5.5 on 'High.'
→ Open the CSV files folder in Claude.
→ Paste this prompt (with your context):

"Be my CFO.

Goal: find every place I lose money, and tell me exactly what to cut, keep, switch or renegotiate, biggest money first.

Context: I attached the transaction exports (CSV) of every bank account and card I use. Each bank uses a different format, currency and date range. Some accounts may be for my business.

Work in 5 steps. Use code for every number: never estimate a total by reading.

STEP 1. Clean

Read every file. For each one, tell me: bank, account, currency, first and last date, number of transactions.

Put everything in one table: date, account, merchant (cleaned: “SQ *JOES COFFEE 4421” becomes “Joe’s Coffee”), amount, currency.

Find the money that only moves between my own accounts: transfers, savings, paying my card bill, currency conversions, refunds. Take it out of spending, so nothing counts twice. If I pay a card you don’t have the file for, tell me.

Group charges billed through Apple, Google, PayPal, Amazon or any other middleman by amount and day of the month, so each hidden subscription shows on its own line.

STEP 2. First look

Show me, for the whole period and per month: money in, money out, what’s left. Then my cost centers (housing, food, transport, software, subscriptions, insurance, fees, travel, business…) from biggest to smallest, and every recurring charge (weekly, monthly, yearly) with its price and when it renews next.

STEP 3. Ask me

Stop here and ask me 5 to 10 questions, with clickable options when you can. Only ask what changes your advice: where I live, my job, who I pay for, which accounts are business, what I’m saving for, and what each charge you can’t name is. Wait for my answers.

STEP 4. The audit, cost center by cost center, biggest first

For each cost center:

- What I spend per month and per year, and whether it’s going up.
- What’s normal for someone like me (my job, my country, my household), and how you know.
- Every merchant inside it, scored: KEEP, WATCH or CUT, with one line why.
- What I’d save per year if I act.

Then hunt for:

> Ghost subscriptions: things I pay for and probably forgot. Ask me if you’re not sure.
> Odd charges: the same charge twice, a price that went up, a free trial that turned paid, a charge after I cancelled, tiny test charges, merchants you can’t identify.
> Fees: bank, card, ATM, currency conversion, late fees, interest.
> Business, if I have...."

PS: I couldn't paste the entire prompt here.

Access the full prompt: https://t.co/38nzKYzEFG.

hits.hook: Hill I'll die on: it is entirely possible to be a great entrepreneur & even greater parent/partner.
hits.original_en:
Hill I'll die on: it is entirely possible to be a great entrepreneur & even greater parent/partner.

When I built my first company, I had a Mount Rushmore of entrepreneurs that I looked up to. It included the usual suspects. 

I was in awe of what they achieved professionally. The hopeless entrepreneurial romantic in me aspired to be have the garage insight to IPO story that united most of them. 

But then I looked at their personal life, and it was largely...concerning. 

Divorce. Infidelity. Absent parenting. 

I wasn't willing to make the good founder-bad familyman tradeoff, but I didn't see any examples of founders that had shown you can have your cake & eat it too. 

This became my new north star as a 2nd time entrepreneur. 

Prove to myself (and others) that it's possible to be an A+ familyman & businessman. And in doing so, achieve two things:

1) As @JoshuaKushner says "[...] be excited to go to work and excited to go home."
2) Provide a roadmap for younger founders to "have it all." 

While the journey isn't over, I have several insights in my pursuit of filling all cups: 

1) It entirely possible to be great at both. 10% of the time things feel like feng shui. 90% of the time you feel an imbalance and are trying to make adjustments to get back to equilibrium. 

2) It is absolutely easier for me as a second-time founder to construct myself in a way that I can have the best of both worlds than it was as a first-time founder. Recognizing that privilege is important. 

3) If I ever feel like I am being a shitty partner/parent and there's no solution/end in sight, I will drop literally every professional endeavor & get my #1 priority (family) in order. 

4) Strong communication with your life & business partner are the foundation for this entire thing to work. 

5) I make sure that I get to do wake-up, morning walk, and bedtime with my wife, daughter, and dog unless there are extenuating circumstances. 

6) The opportunity cost of my time has never been higher. Not because of my business success. But because every minute i'm spending at work is a minute i'm not spending with my family. 

I'll continue to share how I'm approaching my new career mission, but I'm also so encouraged that folks like @mttgrmm, @marcrandolph, and others are painting a picture for crushing work & life.

@Google just dropped Gemini 4 Carbon. It’s a much better coder than Argon—but I’m probably keeping Argon for writing.

We’ve been testing it at @every across coding, writing, design, and knowledge work. It can work for hours on an ambitious project, but it doesn’t always know when to stop.

Here’s your day-zero vibe check:

• Coding: On one run of our Senior Engineer benchmark, Carbon scored 44%, versus Argon’s 21%. A big improvement, though still middle of the pack. In a separate test, @hammer_mt gave it a backlog to work through. It identified 6 tasks as ready, then did 15—including work someone else was already doing. He stopped it after almost 4.5 hours.

• Big builds: @RandyCounsman gave it 3D scans of our podcast studio and an equipment list. In one attempt, it built a browser-based model accurate enough to check whether new gear would fit without getting into the shot. He estimates Carbon also wrote about 95% of a big update to Everycut, our internal video editor.

• Code quality: @kieranklaassen values its tests and documentation on large projects, including its record of approaches it considered and rejected. Fable remains his first choice, but Carbon has earned a place alongside it. The catch: It can produce huge files where Fable keeps things more modular.

• Audio and video: Randy found it caught audio editing issues other models missed. Kieran handed it a recorded meeting and asked for shorts. It came back with 6 titled clips.

• Design: @jackcheng got a hyperrealistic ginkgo-leaf app icon with details other models struggle with. Objects and 3D scenes look better than Argon’s. Interfaces split the team: Jack and Randy kept getting boxes within boxes, while @TylerNishida liked its ideas for new interfaces. Kieran says giving it design guidance makes a big difference.

• Writing: Our editorial benchmark put Carbon and Argon about even. If you like Argon, you’ll probably like Carbon. But Carbon costs more, and I haven’t seen enough improvement to justify switching.

My Reach Test: 🟨 I’ll use it sometimes.

Give it one big job with a clear finish line, and review what comes back. It’s also worth trying as a second opinion, especially on audio and video.
