[X article] how to master fable 5.2 (builder's guide)

i'm going to show you exactly how to master Fable 5.2 to build real features, run experiments, and ship code you can actually trust... 3 secrets. 8 workflows. one feature built end to end.
the prompts, the setup, and how to fix what goes wrong.
steal the workflow. point it at your own codebase.
 
Introduction


listen to me... fable 5.2 can build any feature you throw at it
the real upgrade is making it decide which feature deserves to exist in the first place
and you don't get there by asking for a better plan... you get there by making it build competing versions and letting the evidence pick the winner
take search: full-text, semantic, hybrid... same queries, same constraints, three different answers
most people would just ship whichever one the model sounded most confident about
i'm going to show you how to build the team that runs this, give it memory you can actually test, and make it finish with work you can verify
because a convincing explanation costs nothing... a result that survives a counterexample is the only thing worth keeping
this is the full course
 
what the model does well, the controls that matter, the coordinator and workers, the prompt habits to remove, the memory and completion checks, one complete search feature, and eight workflows you can reuse
 
what this model is exceptional at
before the setup, choose the work worth giving it:
it can test the expensive assumption
for search, the hard decision isn't which button to draw... it's whether semantic retrieval earns its dependencies, latency, and operating cost
build the smallest competing approaches before investing in the full architecture
it can build something you can inspect
turn a notebook into an interactive teaching tool, a reference into a 3d scene, or a product idea into a browser game
map each control to a documented relationship or explicit assumption. label invented geometry. for motion, inspect critical transitions, not just a beautiful still
fable writes code for blender, three.js, and ffmpeg; those tools do the rendering
it can carry the project between specialists
keep one fable session responsible for decisions. let replaceable workers return artifacts instead of trying to share private reasoning
it can use memory without making it sacred
a remembered instruction needs an owner, a reason, a scope, and a behavior you can test
"never retry" can outlive the outage that created it
it can finish against a real contract
"done" should mean the current revision passed the required checks... not that the last paragraph sounds confident
that's the setup we're building
 
the cockpit: every control you need
update claude code first; fable 5.2 needs v2.1.321 or later
use claude-fable-5-2 in an api integration and verify what the provider actually served
 
effort is the biggest cost lever:
low: bounded checks and quick exchanges
medium: interactive coding and ordinary knowledge work
high: hard coding, research, and unattended investigations
xhigh: difficult work where your checks show a gain
max: ceiling measurements, not the default for every feature
most capability gains are already present at high. low scores sat close to fable 5.1 at higher effort; check your own accepted outputs before changing the setting
the api defaults to high; claude code defaults to medium
"answer directly without deliberating" usually worked on 5.1. it does not stop 5.2 thinking at medium and above... remove the line and lower effort
standard pricing is $8 input and $40 output per million tokens. cache reads cost $0.20; five-minute writes $10; one-hour writes $16. fast mode is $16/$80
cheaper tokens don't guarantee a cheaper task: a max-effort comparison with default fallback cost $26.5 per task for 5.2 versus $12.99 for 5.1
record the whole bill: coordinator, workers, advisor, retries, tools, and rejected attempts
 
the main event: make fable run the experiment
 
the role change is simple
stop using the team to build different pieces of your preferred answer... use it to test different answers
the setup:
fable freezes the question: what decision could make the build expensive?
workers build alternatives: full-text, semantic, and hybrid search, in separate working copies
the evaluator stays fixed: shared interface, real queries, relevance judgments, latency, operating constraints
fable selects from evidence: keep the losing case and the condition that would reverse the decision
 
each candidate returns document_id, score, evidence_span, and retrieval_method
give builders development cases. keep held-out cases outside their access. no candidate edits the evaluator or another candidate
"persistent notes" should find a document about agent memory. memory_rule.json must not quietly become memory-record.md
if the hybrid wins relevance but misses the latency requirement, that's a trade-off... not permission to hide the failure in a combined score
before you let fable build the product, let it build the experiment that decides how the product should work
 
build your workers
every worker is a file in .claude/agents/: a name, model, tools, effort, and bounded job
the builder and verifier, complete:
 
copy the exact files from configs/. the full set includes experiment-builder, counterexample-first, question-reader, option-checker, memory-regression, handoff-auditor, ledger-verifier, consequential-specialist, layer-auditor, source-instrument, render-proof, and creative-reference-checker
three rules keep the team useful:
one worker, one question... state which decision its answer changes
separate working copies... no parallel ownership of the same files
no self-graded homework... verify artifacts, not confidence
inspect /tasks for effective model and effort. a file's setting can be overridden
maxTurns is a turn limit, not a dollar cap. permissionMode: default is not a sandbox. enforce network access, spending, and protected paths in the runner
a cost-first subagent tool description cut delegation by about a third on short tasks with the same success. launch a worker when isolation or independent work earns the briefing and merge cost
 
secret 1: remove expensive prompt habits
 
start with the outcome, constraints, and why the result matters
then decide who owns the code
on small coding tasks, no ownership statement or code framed as someone else's produced duplicate-code merging in under a tenth of tries; the rate varied by task
this sentence changed that:
 
merging rose to about half the tries, at about 1.5x output tokens. the requested feature worked in nearly every try either way
but ownership also added unrequested tests and docs, and changed existing feature behavior in one try in six to ten, excluding bug fixes... more often at higher effort
small changes often disappeared from the closing summary. review the diff
"No drive-by refactors, renames or cleanups" earlier in the prompt still left about a third merging
for the search experiment, leave the ownership sentence out. the user owns the app; the evaluator is not the worker's to improve
another expensive habit is advertising a large task-token allowance. removing that harness-written PROMPT TEXT lowered cost with equivalent performance at high and xhigh
that's different from a factual remaining-context gauge, and says nothing about the separate api task budgets beta
 
secret 2: give memory a test suite
keep the project's purpose, actual commands, and recurring mistakes close at hand
but don't turn every old warning into a permanent restriction
 
one never-retry note among about a dozen carried-over notes reduced retries after a busy tool to around four in ten, down from nearly all in simulated tasks
write the safe exception into the actual rule:
 
then replay the old and revised instructions on the same scenarios: safe read timeout, possibly-completed write, denied access, approved edit, and unapproved publish
measure actions, not whether the model says it understood
if the rule blocks every paraphrase, narrow the scope. if it rewrites identifiers, repair the exception. an expired agent note never revokes an explicit user restriction
 
secret 3: finish with proof
write a finish line the agent can't fake
 
for the search feature, require:
the interface stays fixed
exact identifiers remain literal
paraphrases and no-match cases behave as agreed
evidence spans exist in the returned documents
held-out checks run outside builder access
the selected implementation passes integration checks
every passed item has current-revision evidence
the ledger uses pending, passed, failed, or blocked. an unrun check stays pending
a finishing instruction roughly halved medium-effort coding sessions ending with doable work left, with about 30% more output
 
add a real brake: attempts and monetary limits enforced by the host, including in-flight reservations when the cap must be strict
show actual remaining context if the runner measures it. on programbench without compaction, a context display raised the score from 85.6% to 91.6%; without it, 5.2 exhausted context before submission on 68% of tasks
that setup used mini-swe-agent, a single 1m-token window, and no six-hour time limit. a context gauge describes working space... it isn't a spending target
if a run looks silent, inspect the client first. progress updates arrive in thinking blocks; their text is empty at thinking.display: "omitted". render display: "updates" with the thinking-display-updates-2026-08-18 beta header
a turn-scoped reminder roughly halved the longest silent stretch; an opening/update/recap prompt added about 20% output. fix rendering before buying more narration
 
how to build one real feature
everything above, assembled once
step 1, the brief
you type one message:
 
step 2, the plan
define the interface, development fixtures, held-out access, allowed resources, and acceptance checks before touching candidate code
use brief.md, evaluation/, candidates/, results/, and decision.md. keep the decision reversible until the evidence earns integration
step 3, the team goes to work
builders return runnable artifacts. the independent checker attacks the favored candidate. the proposal lane contributes another approach without seeing the others first
for source-driven tools, use source-instrument to check claims, units, assumptions, and controls before drawing the interface. for 3d or games, use render-proof and creative-reference-checker on rough geometry and critical motion before polishing
step 4, the finish line
 
step 5, the review

hits.hook: [X article] How to be a Creative Genius (art of great ideas)
hits.original_en:
[X article] How to be a Creative Genius (art of great ideas) 

Every startup, company, and business worldwide is looking for a cracked marketer, storyteller, or content person. What they're actually hiring for is a creative genius.
Someone who looks at the same market and data as everyone else and spots something completely novel. Someone with brilliant ideas, curated taste, and the ability to create. 
In today's article, I want to show you that creativity isn't something you're born with. You can build it, and I'll show you exactly how.
By the end, you'll understand one of the most in-demand skills in business, and you'll literally start seeing things 99% of people miss. As if you've been handed a pair of glasses only you can wear. 
Contents 
I: The Anatomy of a Creative Genius (high-level)
II: Inputs
III: Capturing Data
IV: Where Great Ideas are Born
V: Taste: The Unfair Advantage 
VI: Final Advice 
If you enjoy this content, all I ask is that you Like, Repost & Follow me @ryangrowthh. It helps ensure I can keep bringing free content to you guys :) 
 
I: The Anatomy of a Creative Genius (high-level)
Firstly, I don't consider myself a creative genius. I'm only writing this because I've spent a lot of time studying and working with them. 
Elon Musk, Steve Jobs, Steven Bartlett, and my own circle of entrepreneurs. 
Most people think creativity is a lightning bolt. A moment of divine inspiration that only certain people are lucky enough to get. I don't think that's true.  
Steve Jobs once said that creativity is just connecting things. The more time I spend making things, the more I think that to be true. 
Almost every "original" idea is really a combination of existing ideas and data that nobody had put together before. 
A cool way to visualize this is as an informational graph of new connections. 
 
At its core, idea generation is the art of finding something new in something old.
In marketing (my area of expertise and the focus of this article), it works the same way. Great ideas come from connecting data, formats, and insights that nobody else thought to connect.
From everyone I've studied and worked with, I've noticed a few key things: 
1.     Better inputs 
They consume more, and more widely, than everyone else. They have more dots (data) than 99% of people. 
2.     They log data 
Creative people have a system for logging information. Writing, visual art, digital storage, and so on. 
A database where they can express their ideas. 
3.     Wide connections 
They constantly link ideas across different fields that seem almost unrelated. 
For example, someone I know created a trending YouTube video on Habit Creation with millions of views after watching a random dog-training ad on Instagram.
4.     Reps
They think...a LOT. They analyze everything in their life in extreme detail and go beyond the surface.
They're extremely curious about the underlying mechanics of why and how things work. Once they understand the fundamentals, they can extrapolate them into something new. 
 
II: Inputs 
Creative geniuses are obsessive about their inputs. The specific data they let into their brains that ultimately leads them to make connections. 
In this section, I want to get practical and apply this to marketing and content since that's my audience, but these principles apply to anything: business, relationships, etc.
One principle to remember: garbage in = garbage out.
Every piece of content you create is a reflection of what you've consumed. 
Your hooks, your angles, your formats, your takes. All of it is built from the dots you've collected up until that particular point in time.
To create better content, you need to consume better content.
Tips
1.     Feed curation
Unfollow accounts that only post noise, rage bait, or recycled BS 
Follow people who are genuinely ahead of you in your niche 
Follow people who are experts in things you're curious about but a beginner at 
Follow people who post original thought & strong opinions 
Follow people who make you think and take new actions in real life
2.     Go wide

The best ideas come from the edges. If you only consume content from your bubble, you'll only ever remix your own niche.

Expand your interests and become curious about new fields.
In marketing, this is often called pulling from "adjacent niches": spaces next to yours that share an audience, a format, or a way of thinking, but haven't been mined for ideas in your niche yet.
 
3.     Go deep

Going deep uncovers novel insights.
I like to think about it this way: "Why does [x] work?"
In content, that means analyzing why a specific piece of content succeeded.
When you understand principles, you can test further. 

4.     Consume like a creator

When something stops you mid-scroll, ask:
Why did this grab me?
Why does this format work?
How could I apply this to my niche?
Extrapolating this to business, creative geniuses analyze why they like [X] product and pull specific fundamentals into their own. 
5.     Talk to real people

Go out and talk to real people with different interests, backgrounds, and insights. 

6.     Balance inputs with outputs

In the context of marketing, this could literally mean that for every 5 articles you consume, you write one. 
In my personal life, I have rules like this.
For every 3 hours of content I consume, I spend 6 hours creating (daily). 
 
III: Capturing Data
Humans have 6,000+ thoughts/day. It's impossible to remember and store all that data.
You need a system for capturing your ideas. Every creative genius does. 
This could be: 
An Obsidian knowledge base (shown below)
A simple journal and pen 
Notion database 
Simple Apple Notes 
A vibe-coded custom dashboard with Claude 
Markdown file system on your desktop
It doesn't matter. The point is, you need to log your ideas so you can think deeply about them later.
Most people have an idea pop into their head and instantly forget it. This eliminates that. 
 
Your system only needs to follow two rules:
Be frictionless: you need to jot ideas down quickly, from anywhere. Use voice-dictation tools, smartwatches, AI agents, etc., if they help.
Regular review: you need a cadence for reviewing and thinking creatively.
My personal system:
For big ideas and reflections, I use the classic journal-and-pen method (I've been doing this for 5 years). At a minimum, I reflect on ideas and goals every month. This is cool because I can literally see my thoughts from when I was a teenager.
For quick ideas, I'll just text my Grok Bot to keep a running log, and every Thursday at 3 pm I time-block to review the last 7 days of ideas.
Public reflection. Lastly, posting here on 𝕏 is a huge creative outlet for me. Even writing this article forces me to think deeply about my frameworks and stress-test my thoughts before publishing. 
 
IV: Where Great Ideas are Born
Obviously, everyone has different preferences for where their best thoughts are born. 
 
Some creative geniuses like complete silence; others like going for walks; some prefer the gym.
But one thing holds true for most: exceptional ideas come from curating the right environment. 
Most great ideas don't come when you're trying your hardest.
When you're deeply focused, your brain locks onto one problem. When you relax, it wanders, pulling from everything you've stored and linking ideas. Neuroscientists associate this wandering state with the brain's default mode network, which plays a big role in creative thinking.
The creative cycle: 
1. Load up → Consume (collect dots)
2. Wrestle  → Think hard about the problem 
3. Let go  → Walk away and do something else 
4. Spark → A new thought appears 
5. Capture → Log the connection before it disappears 
Repeat with your new information. 
 
V: Taste: The Unfair Advantage
Taste isn't something you're born with either. It's pattern recognition, built from thousands of reps of judging things as good or bad and understanding why.
Practical Tips:
1.     Study the best (in and outside your niche)
You can't recognize great work if you've only ever seen average work. Study the top 1% in your field and in fields you admire: the best writers, designers, filmmakers, and brands. Raise your reference points, and your standards will follow.
2.     Have an opinion on everything
Don't just consume, judge. Every time something crosses your feed, ask: Is this good or bad? Why? What would I change?
Have REAL opinions. Don't be afraid of other people disagreeing. 
3.     Build a swipe file
This is one of the best practical tools every creative should build. 
When something is exceptional, save it. Then break it down: the hook, the format, the pacing, the visuals, the emotion it made you feel.
Over time, you'll have a personal library of what "great" looks like, and you'll start noticing the same principles show up again and again (pattern recognition).
4.     Create a lot, keep a little
Taste is mostly editing. It's way easier to know what's bad than to know what's good.
For example, in the context of content, you can write ten hooks and trim until you're left with one.
Great creatives create a bunch, then delete most of it.
5.     Network 
One thing that really helped me build taste was paying mentors to teach me why certain formats landed on social media.
If you look at every creative genius, regardless of their domain, they almost all had mentors. 
 
Final Advice 
Recap
Being an exceptional creative just means:
 Consuming good content → logging your own ideas

If I wanted to make my first $10,000 as an 𝕏 creator in 60 days, this is exactly what I'd do:

(two phases)

PHASE ONE (building a presence) 

1. Niching down (the process) 

Make an EXACT list of 5-10 topics you're exceptional at and understand better than 99% of people.

Frameworks to help: 

• Think about what people ask you for advice on IRL
• Think about what you genuinely like talking about 
• Tap into: your job, experiences, network 
• What do you genuinely believe in?
• What could you help *mostly* anyone with? 

With your list of topics, circle the top 1–3 where your skills overlap with a hot niche. 

Hot niches right now: AI, tech, finance, startups, politics, news, healthcare, fitness. 

2. Set up your profile like a sales page

• Get verified 
• Your first post: an introduction on what you do in [hot niche] and who you help
• Show your face (dox) 
• Write a 3-line max bio of what you do & who it's for
• Pin your introduction post 

3. Warming the account

For the first 1-2 weeks, spend more time networking with bigger accounts in [hot niche]. 

• Reply daily 
• DM other creators 
• Research viral formats/hooks/packaging 

4. Post every day

Two strategies 

1. Quality-first approach: 3-5 high-quality posts/day 

2. Volume-first approach: 8-15 posts/day 

If you're in a fast-moving niche like news or finance, consider option 2; everyone else, stick to #1. 

5. "Heavy-hitting" content 

Repurpose your winning short tweets into videos/article. 

PHASE TWO (monetization)

Multiple routes to take here

1. Creator rewards program

Hit the eligibility requirements, turn on monetization, and do your best to track which posts actually pay.

(Heavy-hitting content pieces get you to 500k verified. Focus on ORIGINAL content only). 

2. Sponsors

You don't need a big audience. I got sponsor offers at 1,500 followers. 

How to land sponsors: 

• Inbound: Clients find you based on your content (tailor your content to what sponsors would want to see - research what they're paying for, then replicate)
• Outbound: Use systems like Grok Bot to find sponsors in your niche 
• Third-party: Sign up to third-party websites/apps that hunt 𝕏 sponsors & campaigns for you 

3. Selling your skill

The best way to make real $$$. Offer a service you're already good at (writing, editing, strategy, consulting). 

• Best pricing for service-based businesses: $2500 x 4, $5000 x 2, $10,000 x 1
• Add a soft CTA to your best posts 
• Add a second piece to your funnel (newsletter, SMS - any way to direct contact leads) 
• Create a VSL/landing-page to push leads from 𝕏
• Run outbound on channels like Email/LinkedIn for prospects

If you do the math: 

2x payouts/mo + 3 sponsors + 3 clients = easily $12K+/mo. 

Bookmark this so you don't forget it.

hits.hook: Robbyant, an embodied AI company under Ant Group, just got a model to read force it was never taught.
hits.original_en:
Robbyant, an embodied AI company under Ant Group, just got a model to read force it was never taught.

Robbyant pretrained LingBot-Touch on 4,983 hours of touch recordings. 

The pretraining data included task-category information, such as opening or pouring, but no frame-level labels for force, contact location or contact timing.

It learned by hiding most of each touch clip and predicting the missing parts in latent space, the JEPA approach Yann LeCun talks about. Then they froze the encoder (the 21.76M-parameter Small version) and trained a small probe on about 2.5 hours of force-labeled data.

On the Sharpa Wave hand, that probe reads fingertip force with an average error of 0.81 N. FTP-1, with an adapter built for that hand, gets 2.31 N. On XHand1, whose specific sensor model was unseen during pretraining, it's 1.32 N against 3.72 N. Contact center on Sharpa Wave: 0.12 mm against 2.19 mm.

The one running on real robots is the Tiny version, 5.46M parameters. Added to π0.5, T-Rex and LingBot-VLA, it lifted mean success on 26 real tasks by about 22 to 25 points.

A probe trained on 2.5 hours of labels getting that close is kind of wild.

The catch: every number here comes from Robbyant's own report, 20 trials per task on two hands. I want to see another lab put it on a hand Robbyant didn't pick.

Touch can't be scraped off the internet. LingBot-Touch was pretrained on 4,983 hours of real tactile recordings from human egocentric and robot-teleoperation data.

hits.hook: [X article] How Do You Measure the ROI of AI?
hits.original_en:
[X article] How Do You Measure the ROI of AI?

TL;DR
For companies early in an AI transformation, we suggest an AI spending ceiling of roughly 0.5% to 2% of annual revenue. Commit part of it up front to infrastructure and experimentation. Make cost-cutting and revenue-generating projects earn the rest as they prove their value, judged by the metrics their teams already use. That’s our 1-3-1 framework: one foundation, three budgets, and one rule for counting returns. A projected return doesn’t count until the business actually captures it.
 
Why AI ROI is so hard to pin down
Imagine you’re the CEO of a midsize company, and four teams come to you about AI:
Finance says its invoicing agent is saving hundreds of hours.
Marketing says its AI video creative has lifted conversion rates.
Engineering says its coding assistant has developers pushing PRs twice as fast.
IT wants a substantial budget for data engineering, with no direct financial return to promise.
These are four different kinds of investment, measured at different units of work. Companies tend to ask the same question of each initiative: what’s the ROI? But the answer requires different measures, and time saved doesn’t necessarily translate into recognized revenue or profit.
Start with what you’re funding, then define the business case and the KPIs that will measure success. That’s the logic behind 1-3-1: one protected foundation, three budgets (experimentation, efficiency, and innovation), and one rule for counting returns.
One foundation, three budgets, one rule
How much should you spend on AI?
Set a company-wide AI spending ceiling rather than letting each department establish its own budget. Individual projects then earn a share of that money with a business case. For companies early in an AI transformation, our suggested starting range is roughly 0.5% to 2% of annual revenue.
That’s deliberately below what established programs spend. In a September 2026 BCG survey of 1,330 executives, companies reported putting about 3.3% of revenue into AI, up from 1.7% a year earlier.
Two kinds of spending (foundation and experimentation) get committed money inside the ceiling, and everything else has to earn its share with evidence.
The four categories
Every AI initiative falls into one of four categories, each with its own share of the budget and its own definition of success.
 
Foundation is the shared infrastructure every AI project runs on. It’s the operating cost of deploying AI securely and reliably, so it gets money committed up front. If the foundation budget is too small, each project has to pay for its own governance, which makes every project look worse than it is and tempts teams to skirt guardrails. Every enterprise needs it, though the range of 8% to 12% of the AI budget is set for regulated industries like insurance.
Experimentation funds teams trying AI on real work, from a sales team drafting proposals under a monthly API cap to a structured pilot on hundreds of support tickets. Treat it like R&D: set aside an amount you can afford to lose entirely, and size it by how many experiments you want to run. A good experiment either turns up an idea worth scaling or rules one out quickly and cheaply. A bad one keeps running without doing either.
Efficiency and innovation are the budgets that have to be earned. Efficiency funds AI that cuts costs; innovation funds AI that grows revenue. Neither gets money until a project clears the evidence bar for its function. The sections below show what that evidence looks like for each category.
In practice: Meridian’s budget
Meridian Specialty Insurance is a fictional insurer with $500 million in revenue, and its figures are illustrative. It’s early in its AI transformation, so it starts below its peers and raises the ceiling as projects prove out:
$5 million spending ceiling (1% of revenue): well below the 3.3% average in BCG’s survey.
$400,000 committed to foundation: 8% of the ceiling, the low end of the range, for a governed data layer, security and governance guardrails, and role-based training.
$700,000 committed to experimentation: about 15% of what’s left, enough for more than two dozen pilots the size of its $25,000 claims test.
Up to $3.9 million for efficiency and innovation: available only to projects that justify the investment.
Fund each initiative from the budget that matches its purpose: foundation, experimentation, efficiency, or innovation. It may deliver other benefits, but count each return only once.
One rule: Track realized returns against projections.
A project expected to save $1 million hasn’t saved it yet. Keep the projection as the benchmark, then track what the business actually captures, including the costs of getting there.
When shouldn’t you care about ROI?
Foundation and experimentation pay off over a longer horizon, so don’t judge their business cases on IRR or NPV alone. Experiments should tell you which ideas deserve more money. Foundation should make each deployment easier than the last. Here’s how that plays out at Meridian.
Experimentation: Judge it by the bets it finds
Meridian gives its claims team a small experimentation budget, with a $5,000 monthly cap on API spending. One adjuster finds that AI can summarize an 80-page claim file in 20 minutes instead of 90. One file tells Meridian little about how the tool will perform across hundreds of claims, especially the difficult ones. But it’s enough to write down a hypothesis worth testing: if AI can summarize claim files reliably, it could cut average processing time by 40%.
Meridian runs a $25,000 pilot on 500 claims, less than a tenth of what a full rollout would cost. Before it starts, the team writes down what results would earn the idea a full business case: at least 90% of summaries pass its quality checks, and processing time still drops by about 40% after adjusters review each summary. On straightforward files, 92% of summaries pass and the time savings hold. On complex files, only 78% pass.
The results narrow the bet. Routine files, about 70% of the volume, advance to a full business case, with human verification required: about $1.1 million a year in adjuster capacity against $300,000 to roll out and $180,000 a year to run. Complex files stay with adjusters for now. That version goes back to experimentation, where the team can test better retrieval or a newer model before it gets more money.
Without that decision, Meridian could keep calling the complex-file results promising and fund another quarter of testing, then another. That’s pilot purgatory. Every pilot should end in a call to scale, revise, or stop. Revising means changing something specific and testing again, not rerunning the same pilot.
Foundation: Judge it by what it makes possible
Many AI projects stall between demo and production on data access, security review, or integration, not on the model itself. Foundation does that work up front, so each new project repeats less of it. It comes before any single use case because it decides how fast and how safely every later project can ship.
Say you build a semantic data layer, one certified definition of every claim, policy, and loss metric, and five agents pull from it through the same governed tools. When those agents start saving money, how much of that return belongs to the semantic layer? It’s hard to say; that’s why measuring the ROI of foundational work like data engineering, security, and integrations is tricky.
But you can measure what it makes possible: how many new use cases launch because it exists, how fast they reach production, what each one costs compared with the first, and how quickly it clears security review. Also check whether people actually use it: whether teams work from the shared data and tools, whether employees use what they were trained on, and whether later projects reuse what earlier ones built. A data layer nobody queries hasn’t made anything possible yet.
At Meridian, the first agent takes nine months to deploy. The next takes six weeks. By then, the claim and policy definitions are certified, the connections to the claims and policy systems exist, and security has approved the access controls. The second agent also costs about a third as much to build and clears security review in two weeks instead of three months.
If an agent saves $1 million, the agent gets credit for that $1 million. The foundation gets credit for making that agent, and the ones after it, faster and cheaper to deploy. Count each return once.
Don’t let foundation become a reason not to ship. Build it alongside your first two or three use cases, and let them show which pieces come first: put the committed money where a missing piece is holding back a use case whose value you already know. That tells you what to build next, not how much of the use case’s return the foundation can claim.
We recommend reinvesting about 20% of realized gains into foundation work early on. That protects it from short-term budget pressure and ties its growth to real results. As the foundation matures and needs fewer new pieces, the share can come down.
When does potential ROI become real?
When the business captures it. That’s the test for efficiency and innovation. A pilot can prove people work faster without the company saving or earning a dollar more, and that gap is the difference between provisional and realized value.
Provisional versus realized
Provisional value is an observed or projected improvement whose financial benefit the business hasn’t yet captured. Realized value is what the business has actually gained through lower costs or incremental revenue, accounting for the costs of achieving it.
Efficiency: Judge it by realized savings
The pilot’s business case put the claims tool’s freed capacity at about $1.1 million a year. But if adjusters work the same hours, staffing costs don’t change, and nothing new gets done, that benefit is still unproven. As our co-founder Arman puts it, “gross productivity gain is not realized savings.”
There are four ways to turn recovered capacity into value:
Hiring avoidance: take on more work without filling planned roles.
Added throughput: handle more volume with the same team, when that replaces overtime, outsourcing, or a backlog that was costing money.
Productive redeployment: move people to work that improves a measurable outcome.
Cost reduction: cut expenses or positions you no longer need.

hits.hook: I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000.
hits.original_en:
I look at what I do with Fable 5.2 in the cracks of my week and think: this would've taken five people and $200,000.

Then I look at what my team does with the same AI.

Last week, between meetings, I analyzed our customer survey, made a game for our team, spotted an opportunity to sell @Every to teams, built a CRM, and started reaching out.

Look at that and you might ask: Why would I need a team at all?

The chart seems to agree. On OpenAI's GDPval benchmark, AI went from beating human experts 12.4% of the time in 2024 to around 83% in 2026. That's the aggregate view of the future of work: gather a lot of data and extrapolate a trend line.

But the aggregate misses something. To see it, you have to get intimate: zoom in on one real situation, with all its messiness, and extrapolate from there.

We gave everyone at Every access to the same customer survey and the same AI models.

• I found an opportunity to sell to teams.
• @poojary_yash saw that first-time subscribers were churning because we send too much email.
• @dabrundage noticed that many of our readers feel lonely: they're excited about AI, but people around them think they're crazy.
• @jackcheng turned the results into a Claymation game show.

Could you ask Claude to produce what each of them found? Maybe. But generating possibilities is cheap. Knowing which ones matter is hard.

@hammer_mt ran an experiment to predict what I'd say in Slack. When Claude got 400 attempts, it produced an answer like mine 93% of the time. But when it had to rank its own answers, mine landed in its top 10% only around 60% of the time.

Each person on a team is responsible for a different part of the world. That responsibility narrows where they look, and their perspective helps them decide what matters enough to act on. A team explores more possibilities than a single default prompt, and it can take responsibility for what it finds.

The obvious objection: models will get better at ranking. I think they will. But people aren't frozen while that happens. Comparing 2026 Yash with 2027 Claude misses that there will also be a 2027 Yash, with another year of experience, using 2027 Claude.

As models improve and spread, they raise the floor for everyone. The default answer becomes the baseline. The value is in using your perspective and responsibility to push past it.

That's why I think we need to change how we measure AI. Instead of only asking how well a model performs on problems everyone agrees are worth solving, ask: How good is it at doing my work, from my perspective?

The aggregate can show us the capability curve. The intimate helps us see what we might build, and who we might become, as we ride it.

I presented this at Thesis: 2027. The full talk is on the Every podcast:

hits.name: Machina
hits.hook: [X article] How to prepare yourself for the next decade of software
hits.original_en:
[X article] How to prepare yourself for the next decade of software

Software as we know it today is dying.
The apps you click through, the forms you fill, the dashboards you check every morning: all of it is getting replaced by agents that do the work for you
they book the trip, charge the card, answer the customer... and nobody's watching while they do it
and the old way of building software is dying with it
you can't click around for a bit, see that it works, and push it live anymore... an agent talks to real people, makes real decisions and moves real money, on its own
the builders who make it through this shift will be the ones who pick up one habit early: testing their agents the way real customers will use them, before a single customer ever does
skip it, and your agent looks perfect in a demo, then tells a real customer "done" when nothing happened
that habit is what separates the agents people trust from the ones they quit... and it's what this whole article is about
so this week i took the agent i use to book my flights and ran it through Plurai
Plurai is a plugin for Claude Code: it creates simulated customers, lets them talk to your agent, checks what your agent really did (not just what it said), and helps you fix whatever breaks
i'll show you the whole run, start to finish, with screenshots from my own screen
here's what's inside:
my agent, and the one thing it must never get wrong
the two words every builder should know
the run: one command, a simulated world, and a crowd of simulated customers
the real problems it found in my agent
the fixes, and the rerun
the loop i'll use on every agent from now on
 
the agent
SkyTrip is the agent i use to book my trips
i tell it where i'm going, it finds the best prices, books the flight and the hotel, charges the card, and emails me the confirmation... no tabs, no comparing sites, one chat and it's done
under the hood it can search flights, book a flight, search hotels, book a hotel, charge the card, check a booking, and send the email
its instructions are one line: "book the trip the customer asks for and confirm when done"
no extra rules, no extra checks... that's how a lot of agents get written
 
and it works: every time i use it, flight booked, hotel booked, card charged, email sent
so in my head, it was ready to hand to other people too... that's where i was wrong
what it must never get wrong
for a travel agent, it's simple: anything that touches the customer's money or their trip
never charge them without a clear yes
never say "you're booked" when the booking doesn't exist
that second one is the sneaky one... an agent can write a perfect reply and still have done nothing
the customer reads "you're all set", closes the chat, and finds out at the airport
Plurai's own blog puts it well: "an agent saying that a flight was booked is not proof that the task succeeded"
the proof is the booking existing - so a real test can't just read what the agent said, it has to go and look at the booking itself
keep that in mind, because that's exactly how Plurai works
why "it worked when i tried it" means nothing
when you test your own agent, you talk to it like you
you know what it can do, so you ask for things it can do... you type clearly, give every detail up front, and never change your mind halfway
real customers don't do any of that: they give half the details, change the date in the middle of a sentence, add a condition you didn't plan for
and your agent has to handle all of it, with nobody watching
 
you can't test what you can't imagine... and you can't sit there holding hundreds of conversations by hand every time you change one line in your prompt
two words every builder should know
if you've never touched testing for agents, these two words are all you need:
simulation: a practice run where simulated customers talk to your agent inside a simulated world
eval: an automatic check of what really happened by the end of that conversation
the simulated customer is just another AI playing a person with a goal, like booking a trip... it reacts to whatever your agent says, the way a real person would
the eval is the referee: it doesn't care how nice the reply sounded, it checks the booking, the payment, the email
 
that's the whole idea, and Plurai does both for you from one command
the run
you install the Plurai plugin in Claude Code, open your agent's folder, and type:
 
that's the whole setup (obviously replace it with your own agent file)
it only asks what it can't figure out on its own... for me that was a couple of quick questions, then it got to work by itself
step 1: it mapped my agent
it read my code and drew a map of SkyTrip: every tool it has and every service it talks to
 
before a single test ran, it already pointed out a couple of weak spots just from reading the code... i'd never noticed either of them, and i use this thing all the time
step 2: it built a simulated world
this is the part that makes it safe to break things
Plurai built a copy of my agent's world where the flights, hotels, payments and emails are all simulated - think of it like a flight simulator for your agent
SkyTrip runs inside it completely unchanged: same code, same model, same instructions
it thinks it's searching real flights and charging real cards... but nothing real gets booked, charged or sent
and the world remembers everything that happens inside it, so when my agent tells a customer "your hotel is booked", Plurai doesn't just believe it: it goes and checks whether that booking exists
same with payments... when the agent says it charged the card, Plurai checks the payment that was really made
 
step 3: it created the customers
this is the part i didn't expect
Plurai wrote a set of test conversations, each with its own simulated customer... and they're not robots typing "book flight please"
each one has a name, a job, a backstory and a personality, like:
a baker planning her trip on her phone before sunrise, who changes her plans halfway through
a manager on a late shift who wants the price before anyone touches his card
someone whose card gets declined
someone in a hurry who wants everything sorted in one go
 
read that list again... every one of those is a real customer you'll get one day
the hurried one, the careful one, the one who changes their mind, the one whose card fails
step 4: it wrote the checks
i didn't write a single test: it read my code, worked out what SkyTrip should never get wrong, and wrote the checks on its own, things like:
did it book what the customer picked
did it charge the right amount
did it charge before the customer said yes
did it make up details the customer never gave, like a birthday or a phone number
did it say "booked" or "email sent" when nothing went through
did it remember what the customer said earlier in the chat
then it ran every conversation several times and scored all of them
what it found
i'll be honest, i expected a disaster... i gave this agent one line of instructions and nothing else
it did better than i thought
the failure i was most worried about, saying "you're all set" when nothing happened, didn't show up once: every time SkyTrip said something was booked, the booking was there
every charge matched the booking total, every email went to the right address, and when a card got declined, it told the customer the truth
but a few conversations went wrong, all caused by 2 bugs... and they're exactly the kind i'd never have caught myself
 
1. it charged the card before saying the price
this was the manager on the late shift
he gave his card and said clearly: "state the final amount before you take any money"
SkyTrip booked the flight, charged the card, and only then replied:
"Your payment went through, and your flight is confirmed"
it did this every single time... sometimes it even told him the amount, right after it had already taken it
imagine that with a real customer: he asked you one simple thing, you ignored it, and you took his money
i'd never caught it myself, because i never say "tell me the price first"... it's my agent, i already trust it
2. it forgot what the customer wanted
this was the baker
she first asked for a return trip, then dropped the return flight and said: "just the way up then. the 11th"
a short, normal reply - the kind you type on your phone with flour on your hands
SkyTrip answered by asking which day she wanted to fly home... the leg she had just cancelled
in another run, it offered her a return flight anyway
 
why one good run means nothing
the baker's bug is the one that should worry you
it didn't happen every time... sometimes SkyTrip got it right, and if i'd tested it once and got the good run, i'd have shipped it
agents don't behave the same way twice: a conversation that works today can fail tomorrow with the exact same setup
your customers don't care about your average... the one who hits the bad run is the one who leaves
that's why Plurai runs every conversation more than once, and why you should only trust what passes again and again
the fixes
this is my favourite part
for each problem, Plurai showed me the exact conversation, explained why it happened, pointed at the line in my code, and wrote the fix... no guessing, no digging through logs
and both problems came from the same place: my one-line instructions
SkyTrip was never told to wait for a yes before charging, and never told to double check the trip after a change... so it did what it was told: book the trip and confirm when done
the fix was 2 new sentences in its instructions:
tell the customer the exact total and wait for their yes before charging
when the customer changes the trip, repeat the new plan in one line and only act on that
no new code, no new tools
 
that's the lesson i'd want you to take from all of this: a lot of agent bugs aren't code bugs... they're missing sentences
you just don't know which ones are missing until someone talks to your agent the way real customers do
then i simply asked Claude to implement these fixes, and ran the simulation again...
the loop
this is the loop i'll run on every agent from now on:
simulate it
fix what breaks
rerun it until it holds
keep every failure as a permanent test
please don't skip the last step
both bugs Plurai found are now saved as tests, so every time i change SkyTrip (a new prompt, a new tool, a new model) those 2 conversations run again
if it ever starts charging before the customer says yes again, i'll know before a customer does... the same mistake can't sneak back in
and every new bug i find gets added to the pile
that's how an...

hits.hook: We’re back to 2020–2021. But yes, this time IS different.
hits.original_en:
We’re back to 2020–2021. But yes, this time IS different.

Wealthy individuals, family offices, and LPs are once again convinced they can invest directly in startups and outperform venture funds.

Some will. I suspect most won’t.

Everyone thinks they have better access, better judgment, and better deals. We’ve seen how that plays out when the market turns.

But here’s the BIG difference.

In 2020–2021, those same investors were ALSO backing emerging VC managers. Money was flowing into funds, SPVs, and startups simultaneously.

Today, more LP capital is bypassing smaller funds entirely and going straight into direct deals and SPVs.

Meanwhile, emerging managers are launching their own SPVs to generate upfront fees, attract LPs, and survive.

The result?

Total capital invested 📈

Capital concentrated in fewer startups 📈

Number of deals 📉

Capital flowing to emerging managers 📉

More money. Fewer deals. Fewer managers getting funded.

The irony is that the very investors who once funded the next generation of VCs are now competing with them for allocations.

This isn’t another 2021 boom where everyone benefits.

It’s a capital concentration cycle disguised as a venture boom.

And when the music stops, we’ll find out who actually knew how to invest.

hits.name: Alex Lieberman
hits.hook: No one knows how to calculate the ROI of AI.
hits.original_en:
No one knows how to calculate the ROI of AI. 

I've spoken to literally 100+ execs about this exact topic and they're at a loss.

Here's how the whole return on intelligence thing has played out: 

1) Org rolls out a general purpose LLM like Claude or Codex.

2) They have some minimum token agreement with a lab and view the investment as experimental. 

3) Time goes on & the company invests in AI upskilling as they want to shift usage away from "advanced google search". 

4) Around the same time, company turns on coding agents for product & engineering orgs. Token spend skyrockets. "What's the ROI of all of this?" convos start emerging. 

5) A short while later, company realizes that a bunch of foundational work like data migration/cleaning & agent gateways are needed to safely/effectively deploy agents. Investment is significant. ROI conversations accelerate & get complicated. "How do we measure the ROI of a data foundation?" starts getting asked. 

6) Company is months into its AI rollout, a bunch of bets have been placed, no ROI methodology has been worked out, and leadership is chomping at the bit for "real results." 

The truth about it is this whole ROI debate is: 

1) It's as old as time 

Measuring ROI of investments in business has never been a perfect science. For some roles (like sellers) it's easy and for other roles (like creatives) it's harder. Same thing goes for software & services. 

The reason ROI has become a fixation with AI is because it's new & because the ease by which you can scale up spend makes the stakes higher & the impact faster. 

2) It's nuanced

You need an ROI framework robust enough to account for the nuances across different types of investments in your business, but simple enough to train your people on. 

Our approach is called 1-3-1. 
• One foundation: the shared infrastructure every AI project runs on. It’s the operating cost of deploying AI securely and reliably, so it gets money committed up front. (8-12% of your AI budget)
• Three budgets: experimentation, efficiency, and innovation
• One rule: don't confuse projected value with realized returns

Read the full article to go deep into the framework & how it's applied in a real business 👇

hits.hook: [X article] How to Run Facebook Ads for Your App with AI (Full Setup)
hits.original_en:
[X article] How to Run Facebook Ads for Your App with AI (Full Setup)

Our app launched on November 5.
Zero ratings. Zero ads running.
One draft campaign sat in our ad account at ₹1,000 ($10) a day.
Honestly, we kept putting it off. Writing an ad is easy. Setting up app ads the right way is the part nobody enjoys.
So we handed the whole prep job to Viktor.
About five minutes later, Viktor sent back six parts.
And before any of them, he told us the campaign we had drafted was the wrong type.
Viktor is an AI employee. He works in our Slack, next to our team.
This is the full setup. What to fix before you spend anything. The exact job we gave him. The campaign he planned. The five ads he wrote. The Meta Ad Library check for ads that have run for months, and how he rebuilds them with AI. The morning check and the weekly report he will run. And the two steps only you can do.
Nothing gatekept.
 
WHY MOST APP ADS FAIL BEFORE THEY START
Most people open Ads Manager, pick a campaign, write one ad and hit publish.
We were about to do the same.
Viktor caught two problems in his first message:
 
→ Wrong campaign type. Our draft was a Sales campaign. An iPhone app needs App promotion, which sends people to the App Store and tracks installs.
→ Wrong devices. Our app needs iOS 26. Target older iPhones and you pay for clicks from people who can't install it.
Ads Manager would have let us publish both.
No error. No warning. Just a budget going to the wrong place.
That is the real problem with app ads. The mistakes are quiet.
 
THE APP AND THE STACK
The app is Lantern, an ADHD planner for iPhone. You dump everything on your mind, it builds your day, and it answers one question: will today fit.
The stack is small:
→ Meta Ads: where the ads run, on Facebook and Instagram.
→ Meta Ad Library: public. Every active ad from every advertiser, with its start date.
→ Kie.ai: the AI image models Viktor calls for the ad scenes.
→ Slack: where Viktor works. We ask, we read, we say yes or no.
→ Google Sheets: already connected to Viktor, for the weekly numbers.
→ Viktor: he does the research, the plan, the ad copy, the ad images, the daily check and the weekly report.
We didn't hire a media buyer for a ₹1,000 ($10) a day test.
We gave the job to Viktor and kept the decisions.
 
STEP 1: GIVE VIKTOR THE JOB
One message in Slack. Six tasks. Three rules.
 
Here is the same message with blanks, so you can copy it:
 
The last three lines matter most.
→ Public sources only. He hasn't seen our ad account yet, so he shouldn't pretend to.
→ No invented numbers. A blank column is honest. A made-up cost per install is not.
→ Nothing turns on without a yes. He proposes. We decide.
 
STEP 2: HE READS BEFORE HE WRITES
Viktor didn't start with ad copy.
He started with the App Store page, our website and the public Meta Ad Library. 8 searches. Active ads. All countries.
First, the one promise every ad should make:
"Know in one line if today fits, and fix it in one tap when it doesn't."
Then, what other planner and ADHD apps keep running:
 
 
And the formats:
→ Creator partnership ads, run through a creator's page.
→ First person videos, 27 seconds to over a minute.
→ Plain screenshot images and short videos that go straight to the App Store.
→ One ad kept for months. One advertiser has run the same video since October 2025.
Then Viktor told us what this research can't do.
The Ad Library shows no spend and no results. So it tells you what keeps repeating, not what performs.
Most people skip that sentence.
Viktor put it in writing.
 
STEP 3: THE FIRST CAMPAIGN
 
Here is the plan Viktor proposed for ₹1,000 ($10) a day:
 
Three choices worth copying:
→ Installs first. At ₹1,000 a day, trial and subscribe events will probably be too rare for the campaign to learn from. Start with installs. Switch to trials once they come in steadily.
→ Fewer placements. He left out Audience Network and Messenger while the budget is this small.
→ Watch the wording. Meta rejects copy that implies it knows the viewer's health condition. "Do you have ADHD?" is out. "Made for ADHD brains" describes the product, so it is fine.
That last one would have got our first ad rejected.
 
STEP 4: BEFORE YOU SPEND ANYTHING
This is the boring part. It also decides everything.
 
Viktor's must-do list before launch:
→ Register the app in Meta for Developers and Events Manager. Link it to the ad account.
→ Add the Meta SDK, or a measurement partner that forwards the data. Without one, installs and trials stay invisible, and the campaign optimizes blind.
→ Set up app events: install and open, start trial, subscribe, purchase, plus one activation event. Ours is the first brain dump sorted.
→ Set up SKAdNetwork conversion values. On iPhone, this is how installs and trials get reported back for most users.
→ Update your App Store privacy answers. Our listing says no tracking. An ads SDK changes that.
→ Make ad sized creatives. 9:16 for Reels and Stories. 4:5 for Feed.
 
The privacy one is the one we would have missed.
Viktor read our own listing, saw the "no tracking" label, and flagged that running ads would make it untrue.
 
STEP 5: FIVE ADS, FIVE ANGLES
One message from Viktor. Five ads. Each on a different angle, each tied to a screenshot we already have.
 
 
Every claim came from our App Store listing. He said so at the top.
Then Viktor checked his own copy:
→ On V3, he noted that one feature needs Apple Intelligence, and told us what to add to keep the ad accurate.
→ On V4, he told us to check the privacy claim again after the SDK goes in.
→ On V5, he pointed out we have no screenshot for that feature yet.
Then we asked Viktor for V1 as real ad images. One 4:5 for Feed. One 9:16 for Stories.
 
Viktor built both from our own App Store screenshot. No stock art. No invented screens.
And he sent notes with them:
 
→ Story layout: text stays clear of the top and bottom, where Instagram puts the profile name and the reply bar.
→ No button in the image. Meta adds its own.
→ The font is close, not exact. Viktor said so, and asked for the real font file.
 
STEP 6: CHECK WHAT KEEPS RUNNING ON META
Five angles were our best guesses.
So we gave Viktor a second job: find the ads other apps have kept running the longest.
Meta won't tell you what an ad earned. It will tell you how long someone kept paying for it.
Here is the second message, shortened:
 
This is the library for "adhd planner". Active ads, United States:
 
About 560 results. Too many to read, and no way to sort by what works.
Viktor went through the advertiser pages of seven apps, kept only ads with 2 or more versions, and ranked them by start date:
 
 
Here is number one in the library itself. Started 16 October 2025. Multiple versions. Still active.
 
Then Viktor wrote down the limits again:
→ Only active ads appear. Ads that already stopped are gone from the library.
→ Long running is a signal, not proof. There is still no spend and no results.
→ He didn't watch the videos. For those he reported only the caption, thumbnail and length.
The same check works for any app.
Our other app is a prayer widget, so we ran the search for that shelf ourselves. "bible app", active ads, United States:
 
About 10,000 results. The first ad in the row has been running since 29 July 2025.
 
STEP 7: REBUILD THE PATTERN WITH AI
A proven ad is not a template. The pattern under it is.
Viktor broke all five down the same way: hook, format, structure, call to action. Then he listed what repeats:
 
And he rewrote three of the patterns for Lantern:
 
 
Our own copy. Our own screenshots. No competitor names, footage or logos.
Viktor set his own rules for the copy too:
→ Never say or imply the viewer has ADHD.
→ No treatment claims.
→ No awards, "#1" or star ratings. We don't have real ones yet.
Now the images.
AI image models often scramble app screens and small text. So Viktor splits the work:
→ The AI model makes the scene: the hand, the desk, the background.
→ Our real screenshot goes on top, in code. Every pixel of the app is genuine.
For the scenes, Viktor calls the image models through Kie.ai. He set up the connection and asked for the key in a secure form:
 
Not in the chat. Viktor never sees the key.
And before he generates anything, Viktor checks the cost per image and tells us first.
 
STEP 8: THE MORNING LOOP
Every morning, one check. One line per ad set.
 
What Viktor will flag:
→ Not delivering: an ad set is active with zero impressions, or an ad was rejected.
→ Overspend: over 125% of the daily budget, two days in a row.
→ Underspend: under 70% of the budget.
→ Cost spike: cost per install more than 30% above that ad set's own 3 day average.
→ Spend with no results: an ad has spent twice the average cost per install with zero installs.
→ Stuck in learning: "Learning limited" for more than 3 days.
→ Tracking gap: installs show up but trials stay at zero for 3 days. Usually an SDK problem.
If nothing is flagged, we get one line: "All on pace."
Two details I liked.
Viktor compares our cost per install with our own history, never with an industry figure.
And these are his proposed thresholds. We can change any of them.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
STEP 9: THE WEEKLY LOOP
Every Monday, the report.
 
 
And the calls Viktor will make:
→ Winner: cost per install clearly below average after real spend. Give it more budget.
→ Fatigue: frequency above 3 and click rate down more than 20% in a week. Refresh the creative.
→ Loser: spent three times the average cost per install with almost nothing to show. Pause it.
→ Ready for trials: enough trial events to switch what the campaign optimizes for.
→ Install mismatch: Meta's install count is far from App Store Connect's.
Every column is empty today.
We haven't spent anything. So there is nothing to fill in, and he didn't fill anything in.
Both loops on one card:
 
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
STEP 10: NOTHING TURNS ON WITHOUT A YES
 
Viktor proposed the schedule:
→ Morning pacing check: every day at 9:15 AM, weekends too, because ads run then too.
→ Weekly report: Mondays at 9:45 AM, covering the week before.
And he stopped there.
Both start only after three things: Meta Ads is connected, we say yes, and we confirm the ad account's timezone.
Same for the campaign itself. Viktor offered to build it in Ads Manager as a paused draft for us to review.
Every action that matters waits for a human yes.
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
THE TWO STEPS ONLY YOU CAN DO
Viktor can't log in to Facebook as you. He shouldn't.
Connecting Meta Ads takes a few clicks, and they are yours:
→ Open the Meta Ads connect page while signed i...

bad news:

outreach messages

building is fun, but sales fund the business and let you progress.
finding the right target audience is the first step, but finding the exact people who could be interested in purchasing what you have to offer is 95% of success.
leads aren’t about finding 1000 random cold emails: real leads are people who actually care about what you’re building

NEVER!

the goal isn't to collect 10,000 emails. it's to find the first 10 people who might actually become your customers!
start small, start manually

4/ INFLUENCERS: Find 50 Micro-Creators to Collaborate With
most founders think of influencers as people with hundreds of thousands of followers and crazy pricing.
wrong.
right strategy: your ideal target is micro-influencers with 2k–10k followers on 𝕏 / LinkedIn who talk about your niche and might be open to collaborations beyond paid sponsorships.

revenue sharing

cross-promotion (in your socials)
here's how to use Claude + Treg to find the right people:
connect Treg to Claude to access social profiles, posts, and people-search data

ask Claude to use Treg to find 50 micro-influencers on LinkedIn with 2k–10k followers who regularly post about your industry

now you have a list of 50 potential distribution partners.

we've done hundreds of collaborations for our product Flowmapp generating hundreds of thousands of organic views:

6/ INTERVIEW: Turn Your Experience Into 30 Days of Content
the biggest founder's problem with AI-generated content?

hits.original_en:
Baidu's new model just built an editable 3D model of a Shenzhen skyscraper by writing its own code.

ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview used architectural references and a visual-understanding MCP tool to write Python scripts in FreeCAD, constructing the East and West towers of Baidu International Building.

Not just a render. Editable CAD geometry, with interior layouts, furniture and the mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems inside.

That last part is what makes it interesting for construction. The same approach could help teams coordinate BIM models and flag a ventilation duct running into a structural beam before it becomes a problem on site.

Under the hood: 280B parameters with 14B active per token and a 1M-token context window. The model also scored 1,668 points in the latest CodeArena: WebDev evaluation, placing #2 among open models and #4 among Chinese models, just behind larger Chinese models including Kimi K3.1 Pro and Qwen3.8-Max.

The API is live on Baidu's Qianfan platform, and the weights are due to be open-sourced before November 25.

It's still a preview, and recreating an existing building from references isn't quite the same as designing a new one from scratch.

But the gap between AI that describes a building and AI that drafts a model an engineer can edit just got a lot smaller.

hits.hook: Underrated life hack: if you want to get deep with someone in <15 minutes, give them one simple prompt:
hits.original_en:
Underrated life hack: if you want to get deep with someone in <15 minutes, give them one simple prompt:

"Walk me through the 5-10 most consequential events in your life. What's the impact each had? What did you learn about yourself? How did it change everything for you?"

----

Here's what it looks like in practice...

My life story in 12 key moments:

1) Created my first “invention” in Ms. Gullo’s Kindergarten class

I didn’t realize it then, but this obsession to create something from nothing became the centerpiece of my entrepreneurial journey

2) Bullied in private school from 5th grade to 12th grade

I didn’t feel belonging or enough for 8 formative years. This built a chip on my shoulder that drove me to “prove them wrong”

3) My dad dies suddenly from a stroke at 47, a week before my junior year of college

This is the most impactful moment of my life. It has me rethink everything. How I process my emotions. What I want to do with my life. The interplay of grief and gratitude.

4) I cofound my first company, Morning Brew. 

Two most important decisions I made. Following my curiosity to solve a problem (business news sucks) and partnering with an amazing cofounder. Being a naive college student was a superpower to build a company. 

5) I quit my “safe” Finance job

I had three mental models for making the decision: what's the worst case scenario, what decision would I regret more, and what if my life ended tomorrow. 

6) I sell my business 

Both profound & anticlimactic. The minute we completed the transaction, I didn't feel the glee you'd expect. But I also knew how this would change everything. My life, my family's live, my relationship with money. 

7) I get married 

Best & most important decision I made in my life was marrying my wife, Carly. She's the best thing that's ever happened to me and our relationship is the foundation for everything else. 

8) We suffer a pregnancy loss 

Lots of feelings reminiscent of my dad's passing. Absolutely horrible experience. I was so struck by my wife's strength & (while not necessary) it reinforced the strength of our relationship. 

9) I’m lost as hell

We as humans are built to create. Create careers. Create businesses. Create projects. Create other humans. When we're not in the act of creation & we don't see a path towards figuring out what we want to create, we spin. That was me. 

10) I start a venture studio 

I became clear about my zone of genius & wanted to go all-in. The thesis was: I cofound a company with an exceptional CEO, I use my distribution to drive customers, employees, and partners. Once there's PMF, I move to the next biz. 

11) I cofound my latest company, Tenex

Two choices have an outsized impact on the success of your business. Who you decide to go into business with & what market you choose. I get to be my full self & feel like a kid in a candy shop, full of wonder, play, and curiosity. 

12) Our daughter is born

Outside of being a husband, being a girl dad to my sweet brooke has been the greatest privilege of my life. It's impossible to articulate the fullness I feel in my heart when I'm with her. 

--

It’s amazing how deeply you can understand someone when they do this exercise with you. 

Try it with your friends, coworkers, and while you’re at it, repost your life story here.

hits.hook: Jensen Huang just resigned after 33 years as NVIDIA's only CEO.
hits.original_en:
Jensen Huang just resigned after 33 years as NVIDIA's only CEO.

He made more billionaires on his management team than any CEO in the world.

And it wasn't just executives. In a 2025 survey of 3,000+ NVIDIA employees, over 2,000 said they were already millionaires. Nearly half said they were worth over $25 million.

These aren't founders or VCs. They're engineers and staff who got paid in stock and stayed. Jensen said he personally reviews pay for every single employee.

His reason was simple: "You take care of people, everything else takes care of itself."

To understand why, go back to a 15-year-old kid washing dishes at Denny's.

Years later, at 30, he sat in a Denny's booth with two friends and decided to build a chip company. None of them really knew how.

Their first chip flopped. By 1996, NVIDIA was nearly bankrupt. Most companies die right there.

He didn't quit. For years he made bets nobody understood, and kept going anyway.

In 2016, he walked into the office of a then-new nonprofit called OpenAI and personally handed over the first DGX-1 AI supercomputer.

Today, much of the AI the world uses runs on NVIDIA chips.

The dishwasher didn't just build a chip company. He gave AI its power, and made thousands of ordinary employees rich along the way.

Honestly, this is very sad to see. He's leaving a company worth more than the annual GDP of more than 180 countries, and the impact he created will outlive any title.

excluded_hits.hook: Some quick observations on Anthropic's IPO:
excluded_hits.original_en:
Some quick observations on Anthropic's IPO:

1/ The number of customers paying $100K or more grew 12x in a year, to over 11,900. And the existing ones are spending about 9x what they did 1 year ago (wild).

2/ The net loss is $23.3B, but $21.9B of that is a paper loss. They owe early investors shares, and those shares got more valuable, so accounting rules count it as a loss (has to do with convertible notes etc being exchanged)

3/ Revenue per employee is over $6.6M!

4/ They did $17B in revenue last quarter, and that's up more than 12x from a year ago.

5/ The stat they feature most is compute efficiency, where they say they get 4x more revenue per dollar of compute than in early 2025. ( I think this is a metric they defined themselves but not 100% sure)

6/ It's a public benefit corporation, so shareholders are buying into a company that's legally allowed to weigh other goals alongside their returns.

7/ You can request shares at the IPO price through Robinhood, SoFi, Schwab, Fidelity and E*TRADE, which I think is somewhat unusual for an IPO this size, but maybe it's a sign of the times?

8/ The whole roadshow is an 11 chapter video that anyone can watch, and it's cool that they shared it.

9/ The ticker is $ANT. It's expected to price on November 18 and start trading the next day.

10/ One of the case studies is about Sparky, Walmart’s shopping assistant, and they say orders through it are about 35% bigger. What’s interesting to me is that shoppers only ever see Walmart, and Anthropic is the plumbing underneath. Sidenote: I co-founded @MeetLCA an agency that builds experiences like this big companies/big startups so this trend is what I'm seeing too (demand for agent experience products)

11/ The founders' letter tells investors to "never let your company be worth a dollar more than it is actually worth." I haven't seen that in an IPO pitch before.

12/ About 250 customers pay them $10M or more a year, and over 1,900 pay $1M or more.

13/ They spent $9.9B on compute last quarter, which is more than half of revenue. $5B of that was bought on short-term deals that cost a lot more, which tells me demand is running ahead of what they planned for.

14/ All 7 co-founders are still at the company, and they lose about 1% of the people they want to keep each year.

15/ They recorded $1.1B in stock based compensation last quarter.

16/ They have about $96B in cash and have raised about $141B in total.

Note: this is not financial advice. Do your own research. I share things I find interesting about startups and building businesses in real-time.

Whether you're into AI or not, this is a historic moment for tech, AI and the USA.

outsiders.hook: [X article] My Grok Bot Content Studio: 1 Bot, 9 Commands, 78 AI Models for Video, Images & Audio (Full Guide)
outsiders.original_en:
[X article] My Grok Bot Content Studio: 1 Bot, 9 Commands, 78 AI Models for Video, Images & Audio (Full Guide)

I stopped juggling five AI apps to make one post.
Now I type one line to a Grok Bot. It plans the shot, picks the model, tells me the price, makes the video, image or soundtrack, and writes the caption. I approve, it builds, I post.
Here's the whole setup, what everything actually costs, and the exact commands. Steal it.
 
One sentence in. 6 seconds of video with sound out. 30¢. That's the whole workflow.
What it makes
Video. Veo, Kling, Seedance, Grok Imagine, Wan and more: 39 video models, most with native sound.
Images. Nano Banana, GPT Image, FLUX, Seedream: 24 image models, including ones that spell the text in your thumbnail right.
Audio. Voiceovers (ElevenLabs, Cartesia and more), music beds and songs (ElevenLabs Music, Suno, Lyria), and sound effects.
All of it inside the Grok chat, on one account, every model at the provider's list price (rounded up to the whole cent). No markup.
The one-prompt test
Which video model is "best" depends on the shot. So I gave four of them the exact same prompt:
 
Grok Imagine: 6 s, 42¢
Veo 3.1 Fast: 6 s, 90¢
Kling 3.0 Pro: 5 s, 84¢
Seedance 2.0: 5 s, $1.51
Same prompt, same key, very different dogs. The Bot picks for you, or you name the model. (This comparison ran through the same Varosity tools the Bot uses.)
Setup (2 minutes)
Open the Bot link (in the first reply and at the end of this article) and tap Add to Grok Bot.
Type /studio. It connects your Varosity account: sign in with Google or email, no card. (The approval screen may name another app, such as "Cursor": that's how Grok registers the connection.)
That's it. You pay only for what it makes, from 1¢ an image.
The connection has a $5-a-day spending cap until you raise it, so a runaway prompt can't drain you.
The 9 commands
/x-post: an idea in, a ready-to-post clip or image plus caption out.
/video: one clip from a description or a starting image.
/image: post images, thumbnails, banners, edits.
/voiceover: a voice track for a clip or a post.
/music: a music bed or a full song.
/sfx: whooshes, UI sounds, ambience.
/product-ad: a 15–20 s ad from a product photo link and one line about it (the video, plus a voiceover and a music track to lay under it).
/storyboard: a short story or explainer in 3–6 shots.
/studio: setup and the full guide.
Prompts I actually use (copy these)
/x-post a launch clip for my coffee brand, vertical, with sound
/image a YouTube thumbnail that says "I TESTED 4 AI VIDEO MODELS", shocked face emoji, neon
/product-ad <link to your product photo>: the water bottle that keeps ice for 48 hours
/music 30 seconds of upbeat lo-fi for a cooking clip
/video 6 s, 9:16: a paper boat sailing through a rainy neon city street
What it costs (real charges, not estimates)
Draft image (FLUX schnell): 1¢ (the 1¢ minimum)
Post image with readable text (Nano Banana): 4¢
6 s video with sound (Veo 3.1 Lite): 30¢
6 s video with sound (Grok Imagine): 42¢
5 s cinematic video (Kling 3.0 Pro): 84¢
The Bot shows the plan and the total before it spends anything, and asks first if a message would cost more than $1.
Why I trust it with my credits
It always shows the price first.
Its rules tell it never to pay. When you run low it hands you a top-up link, and buying credits means you finishing the checkout yourself.
It drafts cheap (1¢ images, short clips) and only makes the final after you pick.
It tells you every asset is AI-generated and reminds you to label it when you post.
Run your whole week on it
Ask the Bot: "Create a routine: every Monday at 9:00 <your time zone>, look at what I posted on X last week (ask me for links if you can't see them), propose three post ideas with a hook each, and make a 1¢ draft image for each. Don't make videos or spend more than 10¢ until I pick." Monday morning, your content plan is waiting.
Get it: https://x.ai/bot/yK6JIfrybDtem7a5VY9bX (also in the first reply). Make something and reply with it. We'll repost the best ones.

outsiders.name: Brivael Le Pogam
outsiders.hook: A lot of companies are making serious money selling AI video workflows.
outsiders.original_en:
A lot of companies are making serious money selling AI video workflows.

A prompt, a model, a template. You pay, you generate, you start over.

It works. But it's a dead end.

A workflow is frozen. It does one thing, one way, and it's obsolete the day a better model ships. Which means every three months.

At Argil, we made a different bet. Instead of copying that, we built an entire AI video ecosystem, with an agent at the center.

That agent has access to three things.

The best models on the market. Veo, Kling, Seedance, Grok, and whatever ships tomorrow. It picks the right model for the right shot. You no longer have to keep up with the race.

Native tools built to work with agents. Not a human interface hacked so an AI can click on it. An editor, a rendering engine, primitives an agent handles the way an editor handles a timeline.

And a system where anyone can build their own apps and distribute them.

That's where everything changes.

An editor with ten years in the craft has something no model has: taste. A rhythm, a sense of the cut, a way of telling a story. Today, that know-how stays locked inside client projects. Tomorrow, they encode it in an app, publish it on Argil, and thousands of people use it. They get paid every time.

Editing skills become an asset. Taste becomes a product.

That's what the App Store did for software. Apple didn't write every app. It built the ground where the best people could.

We're doing the same for video.

I think this is going to be a game changer for the entire industry.

You sell a workflow once. An ecosystem compounds.

The models are the engine. Argil is the steering wheel. And creators are the ones driving.

trend_radar.legend: Trend match 0-100% = 1 - prod(1 - w) over matched 24 h keywords that another author also used in the 48 h window (w: rank 1-10 0.35, 11-25 0.22, 26-40 0.12, curated 0.20). Verdict: >= 50% -> trend; else video/image in the post data -> visual; else >= 100K followers (outsiders without follower data: >= 500K views, estimate) -> author/audience; else coincidence/other. Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.
